div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Great Earthquake.—The appalling tale of the earthquake calamity in Sicily, and Southern Italy, is brightened by stories of self-sacrificing work on the part of the rescuers. Foremost among those to render aid, King Victor and Queen Elena have been working heroically amid the scenes of destruction, regardless of personal danger, and undisma3ed by horrors almost worse than those of a battlefield. But of all queens of Europe. Queen Elena is least likely to be deterred by fear. She comes of a mountain race that has not yet acquired" ners es "and is adored by the poor for her bravery, her goodness, and acts of charity. The Queen- Dowagerhas also visited the stricken districts, and actively assisted in bringing succour to the survivors of the earthquake, which is by far tne most disastrous of any of which history furnishes a record. bicily was, of late years becoming popular as a winter. -resort, for the rich, and leisured classes, but the terrible earthquake will, at any rare this spring, make people think twice before going to the Mediterranean watering places. A Bureau for Womens' Employment.—There was last year in London an exhibition giving a practical demonstration of all the employments open to women, and there was also a womens section at the Franco- British Exhibition. Owing to the many inquiries, it was decided to open in London a permanent bureau which would-afford general ieformation concerning womens' employment—and thus has now been organised and opened under charge of Miss Spencer, at 18s, New -Oxford-street, W.C.—The main work of this office is the distribution among inquirers of booklets giving information how a woman or girl may enter upon any of the employments open to women workers, and in this way the bureau seems capable of doing very useful work. Women Inventors.—Women do not figure very: numerously among patentees, which is probably fortu- nate for them, because nineteen people out of twenty who take out patents lose money by them, or at least never get back their expenses. It is to be hoped that this will not be the fate of Lady Amherst of Hackney, who has recently applied for a patent for a muff. It is singular that the very next application on the official register of the Patent Office is also by a lady of title, Princess Anne of Lowenstein-Wortheim, who applies for a patent for " improvements in self-levelUng cots. bunks and the like, for use en board ship." That sug- gests an attempt to obviate sea-sickness, a problem which patentees by the hundred have tried unsuccess- fully to solve. Princess Anne is a half-sister or Lord lie:thorough. and was left a widow two years after her marriage in 1897. The Queen's Technical Schools.—Tt has been stated more than once, that all members of the Royal Family are required to qualilly themselves in their youth, in , some occupation by which they could, if it were necessary, obtain a livelihood,and it is possible that the report has more formdation than the majority of details which are published with repaid to the private life of , the members of that family. In any event, it is evident from an article written by Mr. Ralph, for a January magazine, that the Queen has a keen sense of the importance of such instruction as will enable young people to tarn a living, and that she has made the way easier for a large number of the village lads and girls, _upon the Royal estate at Sandringham. There is a needlework school for girls, and a cabinet-making school for boys, and in both cases the youthful workers are so thoroughly taught that it is found pOssible to sell the produce of their skill, even to people who are disposed to be critical. The Ring and Queen are frequent customers for articles of furniture which they give away as presents,and so many distinguished people from foreign courts visit the schools, that the fortunate workers may almost be said to live in an atmosphere of Royal patronage, Teaching Singing.—Sir Charles Santley in his "Art obSinging," insists with considerable emphasis, that the person who would teach singine, must himself be able to sing, and be prepared to illustrate practically that which he teaches. The instrumentalist whe teaches

singing, and who reads Sir C. Santley's book may be. disposed to recall to mind how Boswell quoted the line " Who rules o'er freemen must himself be free," and how Johnson replied that it would be as reasonable to say "Who drives fat, oxen must himself be fat." And . , that there are people who differ from the great baritcne . I on this point wns evident from a discussion which arose I al a conference of the Incorporated Society of Musicians, when Dr. W. 11. Cummings and others expressed the opinion that there are men who although they cannot sing, are yet very good teachers of s'nging. Fencing for Women.—lf we would acquire griefs of carriage we must fence, at least that is what French and Arnetlcan women tell us, and of bite immense advantages in this direction have opened up to us. At, the present time, there are several well-known academics in this country,—at one of which two lessons a week for six months costs but three guineas, and the simple dress—where women learn just as men de, and are frequently in a position to challenge men. Many doctors now recommend fencing for nervous pit ients,and it is supposed to be a good and gradual exercise for strengtheu!ng the muscles, and sharpening the wits. i Fashion Artists.—The remarkable height and slin-ness i of the ladies portrssed in fashion books and hellion • articles, occasion us little surprise, the artists who "let us out," and "take us in," as required by Dame Fashion, being old familiar friends. Just now however, these old familiar friends, are really excelling themselves in the matter of. arms. Not content with the lengthy appearance afforded by the perfectly tight sleeves the artists insist upon our arms growing longer weds by week, and the effect in many instance is very funny. Deep Ivory Becerning.—The query as to whether' white is desirable evening wear for the woman past her youth, has long been answered in the affirmative by French authorities, but there still seem to be doubts concerning the subject in this country. As a matter of fact, the rniddleaged or even elderly woman invatiably looks her best in white, always provided she chooses a deep ivory tone, and still further softens it with "old" lace, and if possible pearl embroidery. Repeating the Colour.of the Eyes.—Parisian modistes make a point, whenever possible, of arranging upon the bodice a touch of colour that exactly matches the eyes. When blues and browns are concerned, sush a mode is an easy one to follow, but. it is-more difficult to arrange, matters for possessors of eyes of pale insignificant tones. Much may be done for such folk thoegh, by introducing about the throat some colour that will "bring out" and make the best of these insignificant tones, and a care- ful study of the subject should most certainly not be regarded'as waste of time. Childrens Dances.—This is thechildren's dance season and the sight of forty or fifty of them " footing" it gaily,is one calculated to do the most pessimistic good. The invitations usually hear the hours 4 to B.3oand the little guests may generally be relied upon to arrive punctually. The best hostesses advocate one long table for tea, instead ef several small ones, and put off supper till eight o'clock. For the latter meal, sandwiches appear in divers simple forms, also jellies, custards, blancmanges and lemonade. Crackers too are supplied and cause the greatest possible fun. Not a few American millionairesses, when giving children's parties arrange such affairs much upon the lines of a" grown-up" ball, offering the Small folk the most costly and elaborate dainties, claret cup, snd even champagne, but, needless to say such a procedure is reprehensible in the extreme. Malted Milk.—Doctors are now generally agreed ss to the advantages of taking a cup of warm milk the last thing at night, and those who find this a little bulky, and difficult of digestion, should try ilorlicks Malted Milk. which is more easily assimilated, it has all the dietetic value of full cream milk, enriched with the phosphates of malted grains, whilst the casein or indigestible portion of the milk is converted into a form which prevent's carding in the stomach. More- ! - over it is puresand pasteurised a guarintee against the dangers that lurk in unbolted milk, and being in powder I form, it is always more ready to hand, as it can be instantly prepared by the addit4on of-water only. MADGE.

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE COMMITTEE MEETING
div.p: NORTHERN LEAGUE COMMITTEE MEETING
International Players Suspended.

At a meeting of the Nortiern Rugby League Com- mittee, held at Huddersfield on Tuesday afternoon amongst the transfers approved were :—Daniel from Ebbw Vale to Broughton Rangers ; .1. Rowlinson, from Salford to Runcorn ; J. D. Wharton, from Barrow, to Swinton; and Dan Isherwood, from .Warrington to Leigh. The match Rochdale Hornets v. Widnes, in which ten minutes short time uas pled, also tl:e Lee's v. Wakefield Trinity match, which was similarly curtailed, were allowed to stand. _ _

The explanations of tbe Wakefield Trinity and Dull Kingston Rovers clubs, for late starts at Leeds and Oldham respectively, were accepted. Amongst the retorted players dealt with were two internationals. T. H. Newbotild (Wakefield Trinity), for retaliating against another offender in the match against Dewsbury, was suspended up to and including January 16th ; and Asa Robinson (Halifax', for striking in the patch against Keighley, was suspended for one week. Both players were in the England team against Australia last Saturday.

div.head: gxaminer Satttrday, January 9, 1909,
div.p: The gxaminer Satttrday, January 9, 1909,
WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASH lON - H OME.
THRIFT IN DRESS.

There is nothing in which economy can be more successfully practised than in the care of clothes, writes " Lorna " in the British Weekly. The woman who dresses well on a small yearly expediture does not sit before the fire all evening in her best visiting gown. She folds dainty bodices away in tissue paper, stretches gloves and veils carefully before returning them to their boxes, and allows -a separate shelf or band-box for every hat. The thriftless woman will put a valuable hat on theefender to re-curl the feathers after a wetting, and will leave the hat exposed to the force of the flame tiH a strong smell of burn- ing recalls her to the room. ,

div.head: RESTAURANT INFLUENCE.
div.p: THE RESTAURANT INFLUENCE.

Nothing is more typical of society to-day, writes Airs. Hugh Adams, than the fact that there has grown up in our midst an ever-in- creasing community of people belonging to various classes who desire nothing better than that they should spend the passing of the old year and celebrate the incoming of the new one chanting the words of " Aukl Lang Syne" in a public restaurant among a company of strangers whom they have never seen before, and wham, 'in all probb.bility, they will never see again. It is all part and parcel of the public life which 'appeals co irresistibly to modern society, and helps to foster the cult of restlessness, the love of ex- citement, and the labour.saving passion that dominates one and all alike. Be this good or bad for us, the restaurant influence is one that has undoubtedly come to stay, and one which promises to be even more far-reaching in the future than it is at the present mo- ment, for its success is assured, inasmuch as by setting its own high standard of smartness the restaurant habit has subtly appealed Lo that love of display which is the chief char- acteristic of those women who rule and con- trol the social side of society. The chief at- traction that makes these gatherings so popu- lar lies in the fact that the atmosphere of restaurant life typifies the particular atmo- sphere in which nine out of every ten women crave to live. It is an , atmosphere redolent cf extravagance, dominated by excitement, and by a fascinating sense of irresponsibility and independence. Moreover, the smart restaurant proves /irresistible, inasmuch as .t breathes that, particular air of luxury, not too subtle or too refined, which appeals to the great moneyed class who rule to-clay, and who revel in lavish display and delight in publicity, believing wholly in the creed of let- ting their gold glint before everyone 60 that pll men may mli!P.the valtY4 thqrentt

div.head: LATEST SKIRT.
div.p: THE LATEST SKIRT.

The popularity of the semi-corselet skirt has increased by leaps and bounds, and nearly all the best new models are made with the high top. Our sketch pictures one of the newest and most up-to-date skirts for dressy afternoon or ekeninfi° wear. This skirt hos two seams, one up the middle of the front and the other up the middle of the back. The

corsele+ part it not aAgetierated, but is glJit3 defliq tind. Ii particularly well shaped. The skirt in wry long all round, and is distinctly trained at the back, the folds hanging with all the limpnecs of effect sa i.dispensable nowadays in a fashionable garment. This skirt. would look well carried out in faced cloth, cashmere, cashmere-de-sOie soft satin, velvet, or Ottoman silk. If possible., it should be left unlined, as a lining tends to take away from the clinging hang. MIXED WOOLLEN. FAIMICS:

These are often made with seven gores, fastening down the side with ornamental buttons. They are lined just on the hips with silk, which is pinked out at. the edge and not continued to the feet. now it's 'time you were going home. Don't worry about thwe_ papers." lle called on a certain foreman when she had gone, and next night Miss Teinplo, rode home on a bicycle which wouli hare brought at least douhle what she gave for it, while Jardine sniilfA as he watched her. " She would be mot righteously indignant if she knew," he said. " Still. I expect she neerls. what she earns here, and she'd find it very hard to get it anywhere else."

After that, things „went on muc.h the Fame for a month or two, and if Jardine stayed late at his office to do her work, 'AI iss Temple never sus- pe: ted it. Then one day she came in without the bicycle. and stood before his desk with a red spot on either cheek. " I have given Miss. Watkins •back the bicycle —because I found out why she sold it me so cheap," she said.

Ja.rdino looked up gra7ely. "Was it very wrong of. me?" The girl's _eyes shone curiously, and the man fancied the tars were not very far away. "It was wicked of you to think I would have taken it, and, of course, I can't stay hero now." Jar:line made a little deprecatory gesture. "I should like •to point out that I never thought you'd know,- and I can really see no -reason why you should sacrifice your living because I have done an unwarrantable thing." be caid. "I can at least promise not to offend again." Miss Temple stayed; but their relations were somewhat. strained during the next few weeks. By that time, winfer was dosing in, and Jardine, who noticed that her dress was often wet and her •shoos very muddy, was not astonished when he received a . note one morning stating that Miss Temple had been kept at home ;by a feverish cold. Two days later, he called at a little 'house in a shabby street, and the careworn woman who admitted him was clearly Miss Temple's sister. It was also evident, from what be saw in the chilly room- into which she ushered lm that she undertook sewing of EOIIIC kind for a• living, but Jardine found he could talk to her as he had not spoken yet to any woman. When at last ho went away, leaving a cluster of hothouse fruit behind, Aliss Temple sat down by her sister's bed and gently stroked her hair. "Yon must get better, nettie, and back to your work again," • she said. "Mr. Jardine has assured me that . they can scarcely du without
- A little flush of pleasure crept into the • sick girl's face, and she. did not look at .the elder woman as she asked, "What did you think of him ? "
Miss Temple saw the flush, and her face grew grave, but, she answerea, frankly. "You told me he had a temper, but I fe4 quite sure he is a good man."

- Jardine found his office very lonely during the next 'week, and fancied that Miss Temple • was unusually reserved with him when she returned. Ile could discover no reason,. for this, and tha winter was dragging by when, one wild even- in,g, when he was absent, the gill .stood by the office window. It was not quite dark, and she could see the ground sea froth whitely beneath the crags and the ragged • cloud wisps that whirled above their heads. The little wooden building seemed .to vibrate with the roar of the sea, but a boat was pulling out of the harbour. though she could dimly sac that the men were making very, little headway. "Where are they going?" she asked. Billy,, the zhcck-headed, urchin, who was wait. in to shut up the office, glanced at the boat. "To put the light .on the Ledge stack. It's nearer that way than walking -round the pool." he said. "There's a ketch coming in on the flood, and they'll light up when there's enough water on the 'Ledge. You see they'd knock her bottom in if they run in too soon, and it's just as well the Jason isn't coming' because she'll be drawing four foot more than the ketch, and there'll be a big sea on the. Ledge. There was no word of her unless it was in the telegram." "What telegram?" asked Miss Temple, who had not 'seen any, and Billy rubbed his •head. ." There was one come. but I • dunno where it Went unless Captain Jardine got it," he said. Miss Temple tied up some papers she intended to finish at home, for 'it was a long way to Erldishury, and she did not care to stay at the office too late. It was also blowing hard when she straggled over the high ridge of down, with to rain in her face, but she plodded patiently on until at last, driven back by a deluge, she made' for a lonely Louse. She knew the folks who lived there, and unrolled the papers that were alttost as •wet as she was, while she shel- tered. It was then she found an unopened _tele- gram that had been somehow slipped in 11171011 e: them, and, remembering what Jimmy had told her, the colour faded in her face as she read: "Will be un with the Jason, drawing twelve feet, about half-flood to-night, and lie off until .seiye the light."

Then Hettie- Temple real'-ed as clearly as any cleverer woman that it was time for her to act. The ketch that was expected would be (Ira:Wing ei7ht feet, and the extra four would • make a crrrat difference if the skipper of the Jason steamed in when he saw the light that was not meant for him. In another moment .she made hall"-coherent excuses, and went back into the rain, but not before she - had sizned to one of her host's boys to follow her. She laid one of her very few shillings on the telegram in his palm. _
• "Run all the way to Captain Jardine's and give him this," she said. "It is dreadfully important."

. _ . The lad started one way,--and Miss Temple mother, for she was going straight to the beacon by a rough track across the down. That night it ran water, and now. and then she fell ankhl deep into a muddy pool. The wind whirled her soaked dress about her, the rain almost. blinded her, but, gasping and panting, she held on, re- membering that the Jason would run in when her skipper saw the light. Behind that fact she had only a vague and horrible . fear. .The man who had been kind to her, so she told herself while the blood surged to her forehead, would, if disaster happened, be overwhelmed in dis- grace, or perhaps tried for his life. At last she .stopped, gasping,. on the edge of the cliff, and could only see the red /glare of the Ere that flickered ithrough the spray far away below. The wind roared in the crannies, and the-boom of the sea came up in long reverbera- tions, but she found the first steps •of tho wind- ing pathway, and clung to them a .moment hi an agony of terror. Then, catching at her breath,- she went down. The path was steep and slippery. Wet stones and crumbling soil slid away into the blachness beneath her feet, and the wind that whirled her soaked dress against her shivering limbs strove to tear her from the spongy grasses she clung to, but still the red blaze in the spray was growing nearer. Some- thing tore her fingers as she lowered herself from the last rock. Init she . scarcely felt the sniart, and with a little gasp of thankfulness floundered over . the boulders, With the great black wall of cliff above her. The. Ledge was jagged and weedy, and she -fell into Several icy pools -before she reached the Stack;- and found nobody there. The ketch had evidently 'passed, but the great fire roared and blazed above the white rush of tideway that swept the outer ledge. There was, she _knew, not water enough to float the Jason over it yet. The fire must be „put out. but she Only burnt her finger-} when she would have raked the crackling coa:s from the cage, and the blaze swept aloft mere fiercely than, ever. Still she toiled on with the iron that . scorched her hands, and was not astonished when a black form rose suddenly into the light beside her. She seemed to know that man would be there when he was wanted. • " Not that way! Tear up the sod,o he said. She did it with burnt and bleeding fingers, and still the fire moaked them. until at last the blaze sank a trifle, and Jardine staggered out of the •light. Beneath the 'dark wall of cliff the yellow light was blinking,- and as he watched • it ard cue grew int sight. The Jason -.vas

"More StOn or anything !" he said. " Keep it down until I light the lantern." There was a steamer's red lantern, that was hoisted when the entrance to the harbour wa3. blocked, in the box beneath the cairn, but th, Inan's fingers were shaking, and he struck match after match before he lighted it. Then he saw that the fira was almost mastered, and gasped as be ran the lantern up to the head of a pole behind tha tripod. his face shewed drawn rnd white with a. horrible fear, and the girl's Innbs trembled beneath her. " Heaven grant. they see it in time ! " he said. Meanwhile the Jason was coming on. They could coF her reeling masthead light swing higher through the spray, then the smoke cloud l-fneath it, and a slantzl funnel, until the line of dusky hull grew into The lantern was yet burning feebly. " Oh! " said the girl, with a stifled sob. horrible. They're still coming in." Jardine said nothing whatever, but stood tense and rigid, until a roar of the whistle came ringing down the dark rocks' side. • The ,skipper of the Jason had evidently Seen the fire go out, hut it Would be too late in another few moments if he did not see the lantern. Then the whistle roared agaifi, and the red light beneath the higher yellow one swung a little out of line. swung further, and paled, while -Jardine seemed to choke as he said, " He's pulling over his helm." Next moment the lart red blink- faded Tight out,, and the shadowy hull of the steamer swung WI wart the white sluice of tide so that they could see the. yellow rings of brightness that her side. These. toe. .clo,,ed on one , another, the light aloft . died, . and with her smoke streaming behind her the Jason faded into the night. "Thank - heaven!" said -Jardine, hoarsely. " steaming out." Then 'Miss Temple sat down shivering all
through, in the last faint glow of the fire, and shrank from Jardine, who bent over her. " Let me see your hands," he said.

The girl ;-o—ulci-li;v-e—hi-dden- them, but he was too quick for her, and she saw the pain in hix eyes as he looked down on her tnrn and. blackened fingers. Then he slipped his armn Ghent her, and, lifting her by main force; drew, her to him. . .

" You poor little thing," he said, and, stoop-- ipg further, kissed her on the cheek. Hettio Temple," so Jar as she. could afterwards: remember, did nothing but stand -still, shivering.. "There," said Jardine, - gravely. "You know it now—and I've more to tell you when I get: you under shelter." She went with him, half-dazcd by physical: effort and mental strain, and because she could. scarcely have gone a yard alone. She fancied. that Jardine carried her up the cliff. At last. he led her into a warm, lighted hall, and de- livered her into the hands of a little grey-haired woman, who appeared not unnaturally astonished at the sight of her. "This is Miss Temple," said Jardine. "Get her into •dry things, quick, and take care of her. I'll tell you about it later." '

In another moment ho was running. towards the harbour, and Hettie Temple was sitting by the fire, looking comically protty in his hOuse- keoper's clothes, when he came back. • She col- oured when she saw him, and would have risen, but 'Jardine raised _ his- hand.

" You see, I have taken another liberty—but I really couldn't help it, and there's very little more to tell," he said. "I never knew this nlace was so horribly lonely until I saw yo-a here. That's why I want you to stay in. it for ever." The crimson grew plainer ii Ileitio• Temple's cheeks. "You must," she said, "be quite sure. It • was because you were sorry for .me you kept me at the office? " .
Jardine stooped over her. "If that was all, my dear, I could have kept you there still." "Still," said the girl, softly, "you know I' am a failure." • . _

Jardine laughed a little. "And so," he said, " ara I. Fate summarily closed my career, and I was growing into a hard and bitter man when you came tO' brighten zny life for me. My dear, you were never meant to be wasted on an office." Just then the roar of a whistle rang about the house, and he drew the girl to a window. The rain had gone, and a Llliik of watery moonlight shelved an ugly little two-masted stc.‘amer roll- ing wildly 83 she headed into Eddisbury Pool. " That's your doing," said Jardine, softly. "Those fellows' wives would bless you .if they knew what I . do. I could almost forgive Billy for forgetting to give me that telegram, too, becalm until to-night I was afraid that you were too ,good and pretty to care for such a man as me.' . The girl blushed a little as she looked at. him. "I'm 'afraid I was very wicked, but I scarcely remembered those men on the, Jason at all," she said. "I only fancied I might be saving Ion." - Then there was a ring at the front door, ar.l a man outside said, "Tell - the captain he'd better be quick, becaus the horse ain't, been out fel- e week, and he's doing all he can to kick the front of the trap in." Jardine laughed. "Now," he said, "we'll go home and tell your sister. I wonder what Sir George will think when he hears in the ir'!'' " The baronet, as it happened, expressed his complete approval, and ignominiously failed in an attempt. to strike consternatioa into .the ono culorit, Billy. There was also among the wedding presents a useful one from him, as well as a little diamead to adorn the bride. " It's the most - appropriate thieg I could think of for the .Lady or the Light,' he said.
Cins END.I

div.head: Approaching Bicentenary of Holy Trinity Church.
div.p: Approaching Bicentenary of Holy Trinity Church.

The January number of Holy Trinity Parish Magazine 8a35 :—lt is an interesting fact that we are entering upon the 200th anniversary of Trinity Church Rhich was founded in 1703- 'These were the days when the great Duke of Aler!borough was winning his victories over the French, one of his chief victories, that at Malplaquet, being won this very year. The church too was Active in the spiritual warfare which is her province, having effectually recovered from the after results of the rebellion ; end bad it not been for the disastrous policy sacn after initiated by the rulers of the nation a policy of encouraging religious indiffer- ence, the subsequent religious history of the nation would very likely have been very different to what .it is. It is to be hoped that the bicentenary of the church will be kept in some suitable way. A bicentenary fund. would be an excellent thing if it could be get up.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town r Council was held at the Town Hall on Tues•lay evening, 'the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) presiding. div.head: TRAMWAY 'MANAGER'S SALARY.
div.p: TRAMWAY 'MANAGER'S SALARY.

At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee, it, was resolved that the salary of Mr. John Telfer, tramways manager, be increased from £175 to £2OB per annum, to date from the 3rd of June last. The DEPUTY-MAVOR, in moving the adontjon'of the minutes, said the increase of salary it was pToposed to give Mr. Telfer looked a large increase, but really it was only an increase of ES. By a re-arrangement of duties Mr. Telfer bad taken over work formerly carried out by the assistant electrical engineer, for which they paid • £25 a year. Mr. Telfer, v‘ho was a practical electrical engineer, undertook to do the work for nothing for six months to see if he would give satistac- tion. He bad done that, and durine that time the working expenses had been reduced by £471. Couneillor NV t LKlssost seconded.

Councillor EVANS further pointed out that when the late assistant electrical engineer left them they thought it opportune to make the change. They had found that the assistant electrical engineer could not devote the time to the work, while Mr. Telfer was on the spot and could do it better. The £25 was taken into considera- tion in the appointment of assistant engineer, the Lew official receiving less than his predecessor. Councillor Pn3Am:ft...cos agreed as to the good service rendered by Mr. Telfer but did not approve of the way in which the advance had been given. 116. did not understand that Mr. Telfer took up the new uties with a view to getting a larger salary but simply as a con- venience to the department and himself. The minutes were adopted. A THIRD CHAIRMAN.
The Deputy-Mayor then vacated the chair in order to , attend the children's ball, and Alderman Pierpoint presided.

div.head: SMALL HOLDINGS AND ALLOTMENTS.
div.p: SMALL HOLDINGS AND ALLOTMENTS.

The Small Holdings and Allotments Committee have passed a resolution to the effect that the Town Clerk approach Lord Lilford's agent. and ascertain upon what terms land in Warrington or the neighbourhood could be leased or hired. _ _
The minutes were. passed, on the proposition of Alderman ELLISON, seconded by Councillor WILKINEON.
WARRINGTON BRIDGE.

The General Purposes Committee have resolved that a new bridge he rected in place of the existing War- rington Bridge, and that estimates of the cost of con- structing a bridge ot SO and GO feet wide respectively be obtained.
RAILWAY EX TENSION AT WILDERSPOOL.
THE COUNCIL'S MISTAKE.

The TowN CLERK, at a meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee, laid before the committee the plan deposited by the London and. orth-Western Railway Company for the purchase of land on the west side of their low level line near Wilderspool causeway, and reported that the proposals of the company did not affect any public right. Alderman BENNETT, in movin g that the minute he referred back, said he demurrei in. the strongest' possible, manner to the last phrase. It might be technically correct in legal phraseology, but it was a flagrant contradiction of the facts of the case and he could not vote for it. He bad not a word to say against railway development, but the public convenience ought to be considered, and if that improvement was to be allowed to proceed without the Colporation secur- ing any protection„they were p.actically placing the inhabitants of that. district under a disadvantage and inconvenience which, he thought, as the custodians of the public weal, they ought not to tolerate for a. moment. At present there was no direct route from Wilderspeol to Latchford between Old-road and Fairfield-road. The district in question was a growing one, and if they allowed the railway company to make sidings on the land without protecting the public, the districts of Latchford and Wilder Spool would bo out off by a great wedge of land for all time. This was a matter of such importance that it was well worth their while to go to Parliament and ask, in a perfectly friendly way, that if the railway company were going to make those extensions the future interests of the town should he safeguarded, and that the land across Wilderspool should not he covered by a mass of railway lines without access were provided so that they could get from Latchford to Wilderspool without having to go such a long distance round. The Council had been guilty of tremendous lack of foresight Ncith regard to the widening of the railway bridee at Arpley and be did not wish that to be repeated in this case. Dr. JOSEPH seconded. _ _ _ _

Councillor EVANS pointed out what he considered to he two m'stakes made by the Council in past years. When the new high level road was made the old bridge vtas allowed to stand and it was an obstacle when the proposal to contruct a road from Wilderepool to Latch- rord was brought forward. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., and others interested in the land, gave the Council the opportunity not only of having a road acress, but baying it made free of COIt to the town. That was the time for the Council to have accepted it, and he believed it was too late now to enter into a dis- cussion of the matter. _

Councillor PEACOCK said that six years ago plans were submitted before the Council by Messrs. Pember- ton and Mainvraring whereby they would have given the Council a paved street from Wilderspool to Latch- ford, by way of the 12 foot bridge,but this was blocked by a certain party. Councillor Penbberton was not allowed to speak on that occasion because he was an interested person, but if the Council had had the advan Urge of his remarks, they would not have allowed the scheme to have been thrown on side. They would have to abide by their action now and profit by experience and not allow any party or section of the Council to dominate the wishes of the people of Warrington. The TOWN CLERK said the Corporation had no locus stand% and could not apprar by any means before the committee of the House of Commons. Councillor PEMBERTON said he understood the Rail- way Company had .actually bought the land. The Council made one of the greatest mistakes in their history when they did not accept the offer of six years ago. lie (Councillor Pemberton) suffered by it, but he did not -puffer now. The town was going to suffer, and it was 11 thousand pities, but they could not blame Messrs. Greerall, Whitley and Company. The Council had the land and a made street offered to them for nothing and they refused to accept. What could they go and say to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company now? Messrs. Greens% could say they made the offer and the Corporation refused it, because it was a 121 t. bridge, Well, it was a 12ft. bridge to-day. Alderman 13F.NNETT : You might say it is a wiser Council. - _ ,
Councillor PEMBF.RTON ERid it was no use discussing tbe matter any further. It only showed how particular aVtgahrtnebse e thetfotrheyo Council.ughttoLe in watching the questions bii _ _ _

Th-o TOWN CLERK reptated that there was to public right in the legal sense, and the Corporation could not go before Parliament under the present Bill. The minutes were then adopted, Alderman BENNETT dissenting.

div.head: COUNTING THE STARS.
div.p: COUNTING THE STARS.

Mr. J. Franklin-Adams F.R.A.S., has undertaken the gigantic task of counting the stars and of assigning to each its proper magnitude. The counting will be done from photographs, and plates covering the whole of the Southern Hemisphere have already been secured. These number some 200, and .each is 15in. square, and records the images of from 20,000 to 200,000 stars. To facilitate the counting the plates will be moved across a graduated grating in the field cf a microscope, so that the stars may be counted in strips.

div.head: CONCERNING EARTHQUAKES.
div.p: CONCERNING EARTHQUAKES.

A seisniologist of note, Emilas Oddone, contends that an earthquake, by agitating the whole macs of the earth, may cause another shock is Some distant part where the equili- brium is unstable. As an illustration, it is pointed out that about half an hour before the earthquake at Valparaiso, Chili, OD August 16th, 11-708, e&,smcgra-phs in various places reccrded a sliock in the centre of the Pacific. The time clarsing between the two was approximately the time required for the first derived wave to traverse the intervening diameter of the earth.

div.head: OUR FELLOW-CREATURES.
div.p: OUR FELLOW-CREATURES.

According to. an • official of the Smith- sonian Institution at Washington, the latest enumeration . of the animals known to science includes no leas than 390,000 species. The real number, is believed to be much larger. It has been estimated that of insects alone the earth harbours 2;000,000 species; but the late Professor Riley, a re-.. cognised authority on the subject, held even that estimate as far too low. According to his opinion; 10,000,000 would be a moderate estimate 'of the number of insect species. The number of individuals is, of course, in calculable.

div.head: CAN FISH DISTINGUISH COLOUR?
div.p: CAN FISH DISTINGUISH COLOUR?

The question as to how colour affects the lower organisms is a difficult one, and has been much di,scuseed. Many experiments have been tried with a view to deciding whether they see colour as we see it, and whether or not they can distinguish colours. The fact that many animals are brightly coloured has led naturalists to ruppese priori that they can. Otherwise, they arsgue, what use are the colours? Experiments, on the other hand, give in many cases a very un- decided answer. Discussing the question with regard to fishes, Dr. D. Starr Jordan, of Stanford .University, answers it in the affirmative.

div.head: PENDULUM.
div.p: THE PENDULUM.

Like many of the commonest mechanical instruments in daily use, the invention of the pendulum was due entirely, to chance. Galileo, when under hsenty years of age, was standing one day in the Metropolitan Church of Pisa while some painters were at work on the • ceiling of the church. A suspended lamp which was hanging before the altar was disturbed in some manner, and the scientist was struck with the almost perfect regularity with which it swung backward and forward. The idea of measuring time by such an instrument " found instant generation in his brain, and he completed the system in use to this day.

div.head: GROWTH OF CRYSTALS IN PAPER.
div.p: GROWTH OF CRYSTALS IN PAPER.

In a paper read before the Royal Micro- scopical Society Mr. James Strachan gave an interesting account of his investigations of those curious dendritic growths which some- times occur in paper. These are very moss- like in form, and were formerly taken for vegetable growths. They received, in fact, formal botanical names, such as Conferva dendritica and Dematium olivaceum. In 1872 it was shewn by Liversidge that they Contain copper, .and are purely inorganic. They are, in fact, moss-like radiating groups of crystals of copper oxide proceeding from . a minute nucleus of metallic copper the paper. It was, however, only in 1901 that all doubts concerning the nature of these dendritic growths were cleared up by Scales, in a paper contributed to Science Gossip.

LESS FREQUENT IN MODERN PAPERS. Mr. Strachan gives. ".the result of his further investigations, extending over a period of six years. Among other tliin,gs he answers the question why they are. less frequent in modern papers. The metallic particles from which the dendritic growths are derived doubtless come from the paper-making machinery. Thus the substitution of steel for bronze in paper-making machinery is one cause. Again, dendrites do not flourish in heavily-loaded, or coated, papers, such as so many modern papers are. It was formerly thought that dendritic growths were necessarily very slow, requiring at least twenty years for their de- velopment. Mr. Strachan has shewn that under favourable circumstances the growth may be completed in six months. Dendrites grow most rapidly upon wood and cotton papers, less rapidly, upon linen, and most slowly on esparto and straw.

div.head: COMPLEXITY OF AN ATOM.
div.p: THE COMPLEXITY OF AN ATOM.

An atom, long considered indivisible, as its name implies, is now looked upon as a very complex thing by those scientific men who ac- cept the latest theory of the constitution of matter, says Science Siftings. Though so small that it .would take 350,000,000, placed side by side, to fill the space of an inch, it is a combination of bodies somewhat like our solar system, made up ora central sun, with attendant planets. The sun is a group of corpuscles of positive electricity, ',while the bodies revolving around it are negative elec- trons, each having its own orbit, in which it moves at an appropriate speed, dependent on its distance from the centre. The earth's dis- tance from the sun is equal to 23,400 of the earth's radii. In like manner the radius of the atom—that is, the distance of its furthest "electron" from the centre—has been found to be 50,000 electronic radii.

div.head: TOBACCO AND LUNG DISEASE.
div.p: TOBACCO AND LUNG DISEASE.

The statement that tobacco prevents lung disease eeeme to be true to a certain extent. It is clear that tobacco and tobacco smoke are antis2ptics and germicides of considerable power, (Ind that their action on the pul- monary circulation, says the Family Doctor, is'ueeful in relieving or preventing any ten- dency to chronic congestion of the lunge. Many doctors in various cQuntries have re- marked the comparative immunity from pul- monary diseases enjoyed by workers in to- tam) factories. There are oleo eases re- corded of persons who exhibited serious symptoms of consumption, such as cough and who got

rid Or them all alter working 'or a mut, L. -- bate° factories. Tassinari, in Italy, has proved by elaborate -experiments that tobacco kills microbes, and he strongly recommend smoking as a protection against cholera. Visaiii, during the influenza epidemic of 1889, noticed that workers in tobacco factories al- most entirely escaped. The same thing wtls remarked in Genoa and in Rome. Tobacco smoking has also been recommended by some --doctors in the treatment of consumption.

THE PEOPLING OF THE EARTH.

During the time required to travel from one planet to another in our solar system the germs of life certainly might retain their power of germination, in the opinion of the illustrious, physicist and Nobel prize-winner, 'Professor S. Arrhenius, of the University of Stockholm, who wriks on the topic in the Monig. He does not mean that life could be transmitted from a planet outside our solar system to another, but he inclines to the be- lief that within the solar system we call our own the phenomenon has occurred, thus ex- plaining what seems mysteriouri" to so many— the existence of life here and now. We know, for instance, that the suns in the, universe— there are many—are moving relatively to each other, so that the distance between them varies. We are even able to figure out that during the course of 1,000,000 years some star. probably has been about five .times as close to us as our ncarest stellar neighbour is at present. When we estimate that life has been present on our earth at lAast 100.000.000 years we must admit that it is of little im- portance if a planet should have to wait for the -appearance of life a couple of million years after it has been ready to receive ilk

On the proposition of Mr. JOLLEY seconded by Miss BROA.DEKNT, the minutes were approved.

div.head: RELIEF orF[crt ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: RELIEF orF[crt ACCOMMODATION.

The CLERK read a later from Mr. F. FT. Aukland, relieving oMcer, stating that be had received notice to quit the house 240, Manchester-road, and asking the Guardians to reconsider his application of two years ago for house and office combined. The present arrLa.neetaent was obsolete.
BRo6i-s-s9idtle-opinion of the Relief Com- mittee was that the matter should be left to the Finance Committee.
Mr. JOLLEY : This thing ought to have been dune years ago and would have been but for the stupidity of certaio officials.

Mr. A. BROOKS said the matter was well thrashed out two years ago but it was put off because new offices were then in contemplation. Arrangements had now been made which would probably serve for some years to come, for the housing of the Clerk's staff, but the question of the new premises for relief purposes w4s still with them. He zuggested that the whole matter be left to the Finances Committee. This course was agreed to. ASYLUM PATIENTS.

The CLIZRK submitted the cptorte-rly reports on the p,tients from the Warrington Union who are confined in the County Asylums. The facts were :—Winwick Asylum, 43 males ; one improved ; 12 worse ; 47 females; 6 improved ; none worse. Rainhill Asylum, 60 males ; one improved ; 39 females; no alteration.

div.head: OLD-AGE remsross.
div.p: OLD-AGE remsross.

The CLERK said the Local Government Board had forwarded him the whole of the correspondence affect- ing the application of Charles Worrall, 14, Dale-street, Warrington, for an old-age pension. The Warrington Per,sions Committee were in favour of a pension, hut the pensions officers had advised otherwise on the ques- tion of relief. The Local Government Board asked him to state the circumstances under which the relief was given, and whether it was medical or otherwise. The CHAIRMAN said he understood the question raised was the removal of the man from the local Infirmary to the Workhouse hospital. The CLARK was instructed to furnish the necessary details.

div.head: TAR LATE SIR .1. T. lIIBBERT.
div.p: TAR LATE SIR .1. T. lIIBBERT.

Mr. HOUGHTON introduced the question of providing a memorial to the late Sir 3. 'l'. liihbert in the Union Infirmary. His idea was that a marble bust should be placed in the corridor but he was afraid that would cost too much and he therefore suggested a portrait or a brass tablet.

Mr. Jou.av moved that the sanction of the Local Government Board be obtained to the placing of a tablet in the entrance hall or some other suitable place In the Infirmary. They would all liLe to see some permanent record of the fact that that fine institution was opened by the late Sir John Ilibbert who was personally known to some members of the Board and respected by all. Mr. HOUGHTON seconded and the prorosition was agreed to.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW BUILDINGS,
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW BUILDINGS,

Mr. SEGAIL OWEN-attended to e,xplain alterations made by the Local Government Board in plans of the new infirm block which it, is proposed to erect at a cost of £8,4130. He stated that the Local Government Board approved the plans on Jannary 19th, 1905, con- ditionally on a few alterations being made. The matter was dropped and the suggested alterations were not fully gone into at the time.On December 22nd,howerer, be saw Mr. Kitchener, -chief architect to the Local Government Board, rnd thealterations be wished to be made really simplified the buildings considerably. The alterations havigg been explained, Mr. JOLLEY proposed that the plans as amended be approved. He said it was clear it bad been an advan- tage for Mr. Owen to attend at the Local Government Board offices and confer with the chief architect. The plans as amended would not only supply additional accommodation without any appreciable addition to the cost but would also provide considerable adminis- trative advantages. Miss BROADBENT seconded. Mr. FORSHAW : The approval of the plans does not entail the necessity of going on with the building. The CLERK explained that before the scheme could go on, the plans would again Lave to be formally approved and sarction given to the expenditure, and that could not be done before each Guardian hai received fourteen clays notice.
Mr. FORMA NV said recent changes had somewhat modified his opinion. The old-ago pensions would materially affect the numbers in the House. _
The CHAIRMAN : If you would attend the House Committee like we do, you would find that the number of inmates of the house is now greater than ever it has been since it was a Workhouse.
FORSTTAW I Wag attending the House, Com- mittee before you became a member of the Board. I have not been able to come just lately.
lbe propositi9n wr.s approved.

div.head: enuratton.
div.p: enuratton.
THE EXAMINERS
JANUARY 9th. 1909.

LORD WILLIAM CECIL, who " WESTERNISING " is Rector of Hatfield,is going CHINA, to China for the purpose of "Westernising" it by means of a University. He represents, by his own account a very influential Committee, composed of men belonging to the leading denominations, and of Oxford mid Cambridge undergraduates. The object is to found a Christian University which is to be "a means of bringing happiness to the millions of Chinese now in misery," and of "training states- men who will guide China through the difficult period of awakening and reform which is before her "—an object that is, surely, sufficiently spacious. We cannot but admire the confidence of the promoters of the scheme. The University system has not quite effected in this country what, according to this plan, it is destined to bring about in China. Statesmen, it is true, have come in considerable numbers both from Oxford and Cambridge, which is not strange, however, seeing that they were sent to those Universities to be trained for statesmanship ; but with the methods by which the University system has substituted happiness for misery, and the places where this has been done, we must confess ourselves wholly

unacquainted. We should be sorry to find ourselves out o sympathy with any earnest and reasonable effor for the good of China or any other country; but there is something of an air of burlesque, not only about the terms in which the scheme is set forth, but in the choice of the principal missionary. We do not doubt that Lord WILLIAM CECIL is deeply in earnest; but what is he going to teach the Chinese? Will he" Westernise" them by incul- cating such ideas as that the sons of noble houses should be permitted to conduct themselves as they please without danger of being inter- fered with by clumsy low-class policemen ? Or will he instruct them in the principles of religious toleration as it has been practised at Hatfield, where, until about twenty-five years since, the Dissenters of the place had to worship in a hovel because the agent of Lord WILLIAM CECIL'S father would not let them have land for a chapel ? Or, again, will he impress upon the people of China the wisdom and the beneficence of our laud system, which results, within a stone's , throw of Lord WILLIAM CECIL'S church, in crowding two or three families into one small cottage whilst there are far-rolling spaces of agricultural land within another stone's throw ? The Chinese are not exactly heathen, in the common sense of that word. Dense ignorance is not a characteristic of the Chinese any more than it is of us. China is a country which reverences lea.> tg. Suppose inquiry should be made by intelligent Chinamen into the sort of ideas represented by Lord WILLIAM CECIL at home, might they not be inclined to say that, , whatever else they may be short of, they have no special need of au education in feudalism. It would please us greatly to come across a Com- mittee of Oxford and Cambridge undergraduates bent on transforming misery into happiness in their own country. A large field for usefulness is open. And ought we not to experiment on our- selves before starting out to " Westernise " ? If there is some secret for changing misery into happi- ness, and if this is in possession of LORD WILLIAM CECIL and his influential Committee, let it be tried among the poor of our large towns. China is much larger than England, undoubtedly; but this country is quite big enough, and quite miser- able enough,.to find as much work for happiness makers as they can possibly desire. But if the Chinese scheme is to be proceeded with, we would suggest a little more modesty in the proclamation of its intentions. Large numbers of really enlightened and earnest men have been attempt- ing to Christianise China for one generation after another. Many of them have laid down their lives in the cause which they served. The history of Chinese missions is a heroic tragedy. Is it not offensive then, to say that the Western teaching which China has hitherto received has been materialistic and demoralising, and to- presume that a mission with Lord WILLIAM Cam at its head will effect at once, as by the stroke of an enchanter's wand, what has hitherto been the slow t work of centuries ?

The announcement that an HOLLAND'S heir to the throne of EXPECTED HEIR. Holland is expected is extremly interesting, if only for the fact that hopes of a similar kind have three times before been raised and dashed. All Europe will look with anxiety upon the event, since the luck of Holland in this matter may mean much to the future peace of the world. If Queen Wilhelmina has no heir the position of the Dutch people will be by no means to their taste. Tile present dynasty would become extinct, and the Crown would go either to the Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar, or, failing him, to Prince Henry of Reuss. These two Princes are German, and Holland not unnaturally fears the accession of German it: fiuence in her Court. The German Confederation is a permanent danger to her, and with a German King she would slowly but surely he di awn into it, unless she chose to defy Berlin and run the rick of war to maintain her position of independence. That is the problem which Dutch statesmen see before them if the hopes which are now raised should fail of realisation. For Europe the situation would be equally unpleasant. The independence of the Low Countries has been recognised as necessary for the preservation of the status quo in Northern

Europe. France and England, and even Russi4, could not see Holland pass under German influence without serious misgivings, and mutual interest might conceivably demand some effort to prevent that contingency. So that it is obvious that practically the whole of Europe, desiring peace, will be concerned in the happy outcome ()file expectations which have been announced to the Dutch Chamber.
The needs of the Warring- THE INFIRMARY. ton Infirmary are once more

the subject of a special appeal to the generosity of the townspeople and it cannot be too:clearly and generally realised that the necessities of the case demand a generous response. This is a critical stage in the history of the institution for the completion and occupa- tion of the extension has meant a great increase in the annual expenditure, and it remains to be seen whether Warrington people will rise to the occasion and free the management from anxiety a 3 to ways and means. The facts are succinctly. set forth in a New Year circular issued by Mr. W Peter Rylands (chairman of the Bard of Manage- ment) and Mr. George Dakin (hon. treasurer). It states that since the extension the average number of in-patients has been increased by about 50 per cent, resulting in additional expenditure of about £l,OOO per annum, and the number will be augmented further as funds permit. "The subscrip- tion list in the past amounting to about £6OO per annum must" continues the appeal "be regarded as insignificant in view of the wealth and import- ance of the district, and while those subscriptions were sufficient for the require- ments of the Institution in former years the Board of Management now confidently appeal to all for that substantially increased sapport which the new conditions render vitally necessary. Many have already indicated their intention to make a liberal increase in their subscriptions, and it is proposed to publish a list of these at an early date. Warrington only exists upon its industries, and it is only right that those who live upon those industries should contribute with no niggard hand to relieve the suffering which in most instances arises through the all too frequent accidents which are inseparable from modern enterprise."

During the week a receiver RECKLESS has been appointed to take BREWERY FINANCE over the affairs of Ind AND ITS RESULTS. Coope and Company, brewers, of Burton-on- Trent and Romford. This Company is a glaring example of over-capitalisation, and the ease with which the brewing interest in early days raised money from " widows, orphans," and others, on unsubstantial security. Probably had the Licensing Bill passed, this crisis would have been attributed to the predatory instincts of the Liberal Govern- ment in passing the Licensing Bill, and the share- holders—especially the" widows and orphans " I held up as victims. When the shares of this Company were issued the investing public were so anxious to get" into beer" that the shares went considerably over par. Now the Preference £lO shares are worth about £l,and this after the Lords have thrown out the Licensing Bill. It is probable that on a reconstruction about a million of capital will have to be wiped out, and after the debenture holders have secured what they require, there will be very little left for anyone else. This company 1317 no means stand alone in their financial difficulties. In their last annual report they spoke of the Licensing Bill as " pure unmitigated robbery," and said "if the Bill passes your entire capital, preference and ordinary, may be considered as absolutely wiped out." A financial paper called attention to the fact that this company's entir3 share capital was £1,000,000 against which there was a deficiency of over £BOO,OOO showing on the balance sheet, so that the wiping out process was going on apart altogether from the assistance of the Licensing Bill. Probably during the present year we will see a great deal of this wiping out of capital which was never represented by any substantial security. The" Morning Leader" has this week alluded to the difficulties of another brewing company, in the following terms : " We print in another column an account of the proposals which the directors of Hoare and Co., are laying before their shareholders to-day for cutting down their capital. It is merely impudence which attempts to lay the blame for such a reconstruction as this amounts to on the Licensing Bill. But the interesting—and the tragic —feature of the facts disclosed in the statement is that no less than half the purchase price-1800,000 out of .f.:1,600,000 —was paid up in cash. The' widow and the orphan ' whose money was thus sunk in this gross over-capitalisation will have reason, it is true, to lament their rashness, but it was not temperance reform which led them into it, and no conceivable modification of the licensing law could have saved them from its results."

The report of the Chief NATIONAL THRIFT Registrar of Friendly Societies tor 1907 announces that the savings of the people, as represented by their investments in the various registered provident societies and banks of the United Kingdom, exceel four hundred millions. There may be a grain of truth in Lord Rnsebery's generalisation that national thrift is greater in periods of depression than in periods of prosperity, though it was indiscreet of a Tariff Reform journal, after giving prominence to this " obiter dictum," to choose for its daily crumb of fiscal wisdom the motto. " Tariff Reform will give you more opportunities of thrift." But even if Tariff Reform may be regarded as offering an incentive to thrift by cutting down exaberant prosperity, against this doubtful boon must be set the stern reality that thrift is impossible where there is no margin over the requirements of bare existence. Taxacion ' which raised the cost of the " necessaries of life " I would make saving an unattainable ideal for the poor. A striking feature in the Chief Registrar's Report is the large number of co-operative societies which have been registered as a consequence of the Small Holdings and Allotments Act of 1907. Not only do these societies enable members to acquire their holdings, but they make provision for organising the collec- tion and sale of agricultural produce," and thus tend to a solution of the O:fficulty, which has been largely experienced, of bringing the producer and the consumer in close relations ship.' The S•iiall Holdings Act thus promise. not only to give the labourer access to the land, but to set on foot a movement which will overcome the obstacle which has so long stood in he way of any progress in British agriculure. It has op•n3cl up a new era, in which, instead of a perpetual drain of national strength by rural depopulation, the small cultivator will be multiplied, to the immense advantage of national well-being.

Warrington Musical Festival. Arrangements are well advanced for the second Warrington Mubical Festival which will be held in the Parr Hall on Friday and Saturday, February sth and 6th. The success of the first festival in May last has prompted the committee to extend their enterprise, and this year their will be special contests on the Friday for local competitors only, followed by a splendid series of open competitions on the Saturday. We hope public support will fully justify the departure. Of one thing there can be no doubt —that a rich musical treat will be afforded. The idea of having a special day for Warrington shows that the festival committee intend to do their utmost to encourage local talent. Friday's event's will include church or chapel choir contests for mixed or male choirs of 25 to 35 voices and 16 to 20 voices respectively, children's choral contest and children's action song competition, the latter being confined to Band of Hope children. On Saturday the outstanding items will be the chief choral contest for £2O and the challenge shield presented by Mrs. A. H. Cropfield, and the second choral competition (male choirs) in which the first prize is £l2. The Com- mittee have been fortunate in securing the services of two such eminent adjudicators as Mr. S. Coleridge Taylor and Mr. Harry Evans. Intending competitors are reminded that entries close on Saturday next, January 16th. Copies of the syllabus and all further information can be obtained from the general secretary, Mr. R. W. Cook, 25, Froghall-lane, Warrington.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The Town Council had the unique experieme on Tuesday of sitting under three different chairmen while the meeting was in progress. The Mayor pre- sided at the commencement, but after a while he- left the meeting in order to visit the Children's Ball. Then the Deputy Mayor took the chair, only to vacate - it for the same reason half-an-hour later. The third and last chairman was Alderman Pierpoint, who saw the proceedings to a close. * * *

The statement by the Secretary of Commerce of the United States iu regard to immigration into the States shows how the financial troubles have influenced the returns for the twelve months ending October Ist, 1908. The number of immigrants is stated at 724,112 and the emigrants at 717,814, leaving a net increase therefore of only 6,298, while under normal conditions the net increase is generally nearly one million.

The minutes of the Strea-t linprovement and Light jug Committee contain a terrifying resolution this month. It reads as follows : "That section 50 of the Warrington Corporation Act,1899, which requires all new streets to be laid out, defined, and curbed before any buildings are erected, be in future strictly enforced." Many householders consider that street- making is "curbed too much already. * * * Some very important appeals were considered by the Assessment Committee yesterday, particularly those of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Limited, and Messrs. Rylands, Bros.,Limited. The companies were represented by Messrs. James Dodds and W. P. s R land respectively. The appeals were considered F y at very great length, and ultimately the figures decided upon by the Committee were such that the assessments existing prior to the valuations by Mr. Meacock have been increased by about £4,500. *s*

"The " old-fashioned "Xmas which we have just enjoyed (?) proved a costly luxury for municipalities. Thirty thousand men laboured for two days to clear the London streets of snow, and 503 extra men were similarly engaged at Warrington. The latter moved 3,200 loais of snow, and then an hour's rain did more to dispose of the snow than all the labour of the workers. Nature occasionally gives hints which humble the pride of man. His best efforts are often but puny.

* * * The late Mr. B. A. Dromgroole, of St. Helens, whose death at the ripe old age of eighty-nine occupied on Monday, will be remembered by some of the older Warringtonians. He was a native of this town and before going to St. Helens 56 yeare ago he carried on busioess as a draper in the shop at Market-gate now occupied by Messers. Smith and Walker. In his early days he was associated with the Chartist movement and throughout his life he remainei a vigorous sup- porter of reform and was always fearless in expressing his opinions.

* * * Mr. Victor Grayson, M.P., announces his intention of returning to the House of Commons when the next Session opens in February. We hope the violent and variable Victor will settle down and do some useful work this time. His heroics in the last Session did not advance the cause of the unemployed to any per- ceptible extent, and they resulted in his constituency being the disfranchised for time being. Just as Rome was not built in a day, unemployment cannot be remedied in five minutes. Messina should furnish as good an object lesson as Rome, i.e. that it is easier to destroy than create.

The Town Council usually seizes with avidity upon. any opportunity to have a hearty laugh during debate. On Tuesday, however, the members, including the victim and the innocent perpetrator, missed one really excellent joke, It was at the expense of Alderman Bennett, who not infrequently suffers from other people's misdirected sense of humour. In this case the humour was unconscious. Alderman Tinnion was speaking about the checking of accounts by the Watch Committee, when he said " Alderman Bennett knows something about it ; it is donkey work ! " The Council missed the point, and we had the laugh all to ourselves. We would rather have shared it.

* * * Two touching instances of gratitude and self-denial on the part of old-age pensioners have been reported. In one of the offertory bags at Saffron Wallin parish church on Sunday was found a piece of paper,in which had been carefully wrapped ss. An accompanying note stated that the ss. was the first payment received under the Old-Age Pension Act, and that it was given to the church as a thankoffering. The " Christian Commonwealth "this week contains a letter from " A Poor Widow," who encloses her first old-age pension as a contribution towards the Social Service Fund of the Progressive League, of which the Rev. R. J. Campbell, ALA., is president. The letter is as follows : I have so often longed to do something to help the poor children, but have not been able to do so ; but decided, if ever I received the old-age pension I would send them the first five shillings, and I have to-day received that, and ask you if you will kindly see to it for me, and may God bless and help them and you in your good work.—A POOII WIDOW. * * * You can have a regiment of good business qualities, and still fail without courage.—G. ll.Lorrimore. The intelligent man finds almost everything ridiculous; the sensible man hardly anything.— Goethe. _ _
Enough and too much of the sect and the name; What matters our label so truth be our aim. Whittler.
Comparing man and woman generally, one may say that woman would not have the genius for adornment if she had not the instinct for the secondary rOle.--Friedrich Nietzsche. ___

Riches, one may say, are like sea-water; the mor you drink the thirstier you become.—Schopenhatter. Mankind are unco' weak, and little to be trusted; If self the wavering balance shake, it's rarely right adjusted. —Robert Burns. Some people are so much easier to get on with when they are mad than when they are sane.— G. B. Burgin. * * *

Not many people have seen Councillor Pemberton turn tail and run. Pugnacity is one of his strong points and if any man can be relied upon to keep his face to the foe it is John Pemberton. But on Wed- nesday morning he met a foe from whom he fled with- out troubling about the order of his going. The foe had a knife and made a slash at Councillor Pemberton without a moment's warning. Our friend dodged the blow and then negotiated the staircase behind him with unheard of rapidity. Councillor Pemberton informs us that he never came downstairs so fast in his life. A madman with a knife in the rear makes a wonderful accelerator. These exciting incidents occurred in the office of Councillor Steel, who himself had a very narrow escape as the man threatened to murder him first and then turned on Councillor Pemberton when the latter tried a little calm and gentle reasoning. He seemed to be wrought to a frenzy by some real or imagined grievance against the solicitor, and both Councillors are to be congratu- lated on their narrow escape from serious, if not mortal injury. * * *

The Channel has been swam—in America. Our readers will doubtless have seen statements in English papers that a Boston, Mass, newspaper recently published thrilling accounts of an American swimmer's success in swimming the Channel. Curiously enough nothing was known of the achievement here. Perhaps the Yankee hero performed the feat in the dead of night on the sly. Anyhow the descriptive details are typically American. The chronicler, one Hamblin, thus describes the finish. Mahony's legs were useless, but his arms were still going grand. Mahony turned over on his breast and used a double overarm stroke, trailing his legs. About 100 yards from shore I pulled up beside him and, wrenching the American flag from the stern of the boat, handed it to the swimmer, and shouted," Carry it ashore and plant it in Old England." He took the flag. In half a dozen strokes he would touch the bottom. His legs refused to support him, and he fell twice, but he staggered on. When in water up to his waist a wave a foot and a half high knocked him over.. He clung to the flag and stumbled on, half swimming and half walking, until he took the flag ashore, where he went down_ for good, and the greatest
swim on record was finished. . Holbein, Burgess and Co., must feel that the one thing lacking in their case was the Stars and Stripes.

OUGHT I TO lISB GIASSES.—In order to answer this question it is necessary to test the sight. This is done and all information given willingly. JOHNSTON WATSON, Eyesight Testing Rooms, 84, Brldge-street, Warrington. Hours of Business: 9.30 to 730. Johnston Watson attends on Monday and Tuesday from 11 to 4.30, Wednesday 11 to '5.30. Tharday 11 to 1, and Friday and Saturday 11th s.3o.—Advt.

M. a P. Greg, a well known Cheshire magistrate awl property-owner and a prominent leader of the Liberal forces in Mr. A. J. King M.P.'s constituency of Knutsford, has just made an interesting regulation regarding the management of the hostelry os his estate. He has caused the following notice to be dis- played in the hotel :—" I have given instructions that no one is to be served with more than two glasses of intoxicating liquor at a time.—H. P. GREG." The matter is naturally arousing much discussion in the district and particularly among the clientele of Mr. Greg's hotel. Some of these gentlemen will doubtless feel aggrieved as such a curtailment of the liberty of the subject, but the only rights concerned are those of Mr. Greg. We shalt be sympathetically interested in seeing how his compulsory temperance scheme works. Just Imagine the outcry from the brewer and consumer if the State imposed such a regulation! * * More reasons for the reform of the House of Lords! A declared lunatic (writes a " Westminster Gazette " correspondent) is, as you have correctly stated, if an Irish Representative Peer, irremovable from the House of Lords. He is equally secare in his seat in that assembly if be hold it by hereditary right as a Peer of the United Kingdom. A seat in the House of Commons is vacated by lunacy. To the House of Lords a Peer has been brought from a lunatic asylum to take part in a division of critical import ; and a ' Peer who has been declared judicially to be incapable of managing his own private affairs cannot be pre- cluded from managing the affairs of the nation. Similarly a seat in the House of Commons is instantly vacated on conviction of felony. A Peer convicted of felony by his Peers can sit in the House of Lords, and vote and take part in its discussions. A member of the House of Commons can be expelled for mis- conduct within its walls or without. The House of Lords has no such power. * * " The Nation" makes some interesting observations on Lord Rosebery's recant address on thrift at Edinburgh, and contrasts saving with the "genius for speculation." "Take the case cited by Lord Rosebery himself, that of Mr. Andrew Carnegie, or of a lad who lauded in South Carolina 63 years ago with 12s. in his pocket, and died leaving ten million sterling Yesterday. It is not the personal self-sacrifice of milli )naires that works these modern marvels, as Mr. Carnegie, in his singularly frank dis- sussion of the origins of wealth, admits. It lies largely in the great capitalist's Power to buy the capital and labour of others, and to !ell the product as dear as it can be profitably made, 155' cornering' natural sources of supply, repress- ng Competition, securing preferences on railroads, extracting tariffs from governments, and utilising yery weapon of economic force which comes within ins reach. To suggest to the simple working man who Puts some savings in the Edinburgh Savings Bank .that be is fairly on his way to become a Rockefeller, is to ignore all the most salient features in our modern economy."

* * * Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., resigned the Mastership of the Belvoir Hunt bennse, so he said, he would not be able to continue the expense if the Licensing Bill became law. When the Lords threw out the Bill a great load was.presumably removed from the Knight of Walton's mind, for he immediately withdrew the .Tesignation and resumed command of the Belvoir. e..`,Tevc we learn of another resignation. Lord Charles Bentinck has tendered his resignation of the Master- ship of the Blanknev Hunt, for the sole reason that -there is a scarcity of foxes. He has been asked to reconsider his decision and those passing the resolu- tion pledged themselves to do their utmost to improve the Supply of foxes. It really seems as if we had another depressed industry on our hands. Perhaps -the Tariff Reformers can suggest a remedy. In the meantime, however, it is suggested that the remedy which the Blankney Hunt subscribers have pledged themselves to carry out is nothing less than an Import of foreign go-Kls in order to improve the home IndustrY—an action which must be a severe strain Upon the consciences of the Tariff Reformers among the Hunt subscribers. Even the.Blankney Hunt will apparently have to testify,unwillingly,to the benefits of Free Trade, for there is no tax that we are aware of on -imported foxes.
