div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Corning Events.

At the Penny popular concert at Bold-street school this (Saturday) evening an attractive programme arranged by Mr. Levi Richardson will be submitted. At Wycliffe Church to-morrow (Sunday) evening, the Rev. John Yonge will preach a New Year's sermon to young men. l'he members of Legh-street Primitive Methodist Choir will render the cantata "Esther, the Beautiful Queen" at Golborne-street Baptist Church on Thurs- dFund ay evening next, in aid of the Baptist Extension The Parliamentary Debating Society resumes its debates at the Assembly Room, Sankey-street, on Thursday evening next at 7.45. The first annual meeting in connection with the Warrington Adult School will he' held in Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Saturday evening next. Mr. C. E. Parker will preside and addresses will be delivered by Mr. J.F. Gillman(Secretary of the Yorkshire Addl School Union), and others. In connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, a meeting will be held at the Liberal Club on Monday evening, January 25th, when an address will be delivered by Mrs. Sara Andrews (of Manchester), on "Infant Mortality." A Soiree promoted bv the Women's Libera Association will be held in the Lion Hotel rooms on Friday, February 19th. Tocornmemorate the opening of the new Central Premises of the Warrington Co-operative Society, a tea, concert and dance will be held in the Parr Hall on Thursday January 28th. A most attractive pro- gramme is announced. Full particulars appear in our advertising Columns* PUBLIC BEWEFIT.—UNDER TUE CLOCK FOR: BEST BOOTS IN LANCASIIIRE.—Advt, Warrington Chamber of Commerce. At the annual meeting of the Associated Chambers the Warrington to be held in London in March next, tun Warrington Chamber will move the LllolNing resolution :—" That this Association approves of the proposed " Daylight Saving Bill," and, believing that the adoption of the principles therein embodied would be of incalculable benefit to the community generally, and especially to those engaged in Commerce and I_ndustry, desires to express the hope that his Majesty's Government may give their early attention to the measure ; and that a recommendation to this effect be forwarded to the President of the Borad of Trade."— We understand that the Manchester Chamber has promised to second the resolution, and that the 'Principle which it embodies is warmly supported by many other leading Chambers throughout the country -Table Floor, and Hanging LAMPS.. Latestaesigns n..oxv showing. See windows.—J. S. GARLAND, 51- 05, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. 'Warrington Distress Committee. The annual meeting of the Distress Committee was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Monday evening. At the outset the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Rollaway), presided. There were also present Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Mrs. Simpson, the Revs. W. Bracecamp and John Yonge, Alderman Tinnion, Councillors Wilson, Lashford, and Broadhurst, and Messrs. A. J. Jolley, W. Gill, T. P. Bradshaw, John Haley, Robert Lee, T. H. Spinks (assistant town clerk), and J. Fargber (Labour Bureau inquiry officer).—On the motion of Mr. Jolley, seconded by the Rev. W. Bracecamp, Alderman Tinnion was re-elected chair- man of the committee for the ensuing year.—The Chairman in returning thanks referred to the good work of the committee in bringing employers and er9loyes together. They had no public fund, or 'Private subscriptions, but the money they had, £2OO, had been exceedingly well spent.—On the proposition of the Rev. W. Bracecamp, seconded by Councillor Wilson, Mr. A. J Jolley was app inted 'deputy chairman. the following committees were elected :—Finance and General Purposes : Councillors Evans, Dr. Joseph, Pemberton and Wilkinson, Miss Constance Broadbent, Mrs. Joseph Barrison, Mr. T. P. Bradshaw, Mr, W. C. Brooks and Mr. Robert Lee.--- Inquiry and Labour: Councillors Barton, Dickenson, Skelland, Toole, Wilkinson, and 1,118°12, Mrs. Agnes Simpson, Mrs. Al. J. Wilkinson, 41r. Robert Bolton, Mr. William Gill, Mr. R. Lee, the TRev. W. Bracecamp' Mr. John Haley, Rev. John nnge, and Councillors Lashford and Broadhurst.-- private discussion took place on the prevailing 'tress in the borough and the Chairman was quested to bring the matter under the notice of the Council with a view to useful public work 'lug undertaken.

The Savings Bank . Important changes in the hours of business at the Warrington Savings Bank, Batternaarket-street, are announced in our advertising columns. The Bank will now be open as follows : —Monday from 10 to 3 ; Tuesday, 10 to 3; Wednesday, 10 to 4; Thursday, 10 to 1 ; Friday, 10 to 3; Saturday, 10 to 1 ; Saturday evening, 6to 8. One shilling will open an account and there is no charge for books. Novel Competition. An advertisement in another column announces that a cash prize of half a guinea will be awarded for the best title of the bazaar in aid of Warrington Baptist Church Extension Funds to be held in the Parr Hall from liarch 24th to 27th. The bazaar will be of a scenic character. Each suggested title,with an entrance fee of 6c1., must be forwarded to Aldermaa Bennet, of the Market Gate Chambers. Union Bank of Manchester, Ltd. The net profits of the Union Bank of Manchester, Limited, for the half-year ended 31st December, 1903, including £11,132 brought forward, amount to £49,557. The Directors have declared the usual dividend of 12s. per share, absorbing £30,090 and have transferred £2,000 to Premises Reduction Account, £2,500 to Pension Fund, and £5,000 to Reserve Fund (raising that Fund to £355,000), eaving the amouat to be carried forward, £10,057. The Official Receiver's Report. Mr. J. Grant Gibson, Official Receiver for Man- chester, Salford, Warrington, and Ashton-under-Lyne, reports that in the past year 149 receiving orders were made in the district, as against 112 in 1907. There were also five winding-up orders in the company cases. Dividends were paid in 57 cases, but in 47 cases the assets only amounted to £551 and the costs were £527. For the third year in saccessioa the auctioneers and agents employed to realise debtors' estates have obtained more for them than the debtors themselves estimated their value at. PUBLIC BENEFIT UNDER TIIS CLOCK FORBEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

How the Pension Went. At the Borough Police Court on Siturday, Owen Tangy, of no settled abode was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Roome-street at 9 30 on Friday night. A colour-sergeant from Orford Barracks stated that prisoner was very disorderly on the Barracks Square,and was swinging a bottle round. Lie was put out but. persisted in returning and created another scene.—The Chief Constable stated that prisoner had been in the Army, and the previous day he drew a pension of £2 65., and when he was locked up he only had 31d. in his possession. Shire Horse Suffocated. The Warrington Fire Brigade received a call on Sunday evening to a fire which had broken out in a stable on the farm premises of Mr. Albert Percival, Stretton House, Stretton. The Deputy Superintendent (Mr. Frank Turner) and a full complement of men were promptly on the scene, but on their arrival at the farm,found that the flames had been extinguished. They had broken out in a stable in which a very valuable shire stallion, Carbine, was kept, and the animal was suffocated by the smoke. Otherwise, little damage was done. A Pair of " DOULTON ORNA:MENTS make a choice and acceptable present. Stock ranges from 5. to £5 per pair.—J. S. GIRLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Death of an Old-age Pensioner. Mr. Thomas Lawley, of Lymn3, who on Friday received his old-age pension, died whilst having his breakfast on Saturday. Mr. Liwley was within a month of the great age of 81, and in his young days be went to the same school as the late Bishop Frazer. He was with the Duke of Sutherland at Trentham for a term, and some 28 years ago went to Lymm and carried on the Plough Hotel Livery stables until his retirement from active work. Thr funeral took place at the Lymni Parish Church on Monday, the service being taken by the Rector. Many beautiful, floral tributes were forwarded.
COAGOLINE," KLINX," TEXASHINE.' Cements for mending all things.—Advt. Christmas Work for the Unemployed.

The Postmaster this Christmas has shown his sympathy for the unemployed in every practicable manner, and his desire to assist the work of the Labour Bureau by taking the men from the register for his Christmas auxiliary duties. He expressed a wish that preference should be given to married men, and that the work should ba distributed amongst as many men as possible who had suitable references. An opportunity of employment was offered to 66 men, 10 of whom since registration had been fortunate enough to obtain situations, and 56 were given employment. The men were very grateful for the opportunity afforded them of earning something for the Christmas cheer.

The Dandy Mllitalres. From our advertising columns it will be seen that our townsman Mr. Matt Kilduff is bringing his cele- brated Dandy Militaires, high class and refined entertainers, to the Parr Hall next week. This is the first time the troupe has been on tour and so far it has met with great success. The company includes several arsistes uho are well known in the profession and they have given upwards of 2,000 performances at the Pavilion, Frizingliall, Bradford, where they have attracted enormous crowds. At the concluding performances there last October every available seat was booked a fortnight in advance. Mr. Kilduff is now the sole proprietor of the Pavilion. No doubt many of his admirers, especially his old associates of the St. Mary's Dramatic Society, will renew old acquaintances next week. There w'll be a matinee on Saturday afternoon.
LINSEED COMPOUND' (Aniseed, Senega, Squill &e.), for Coughs. Of Chemists only.—Advt.
Buckley-street Sunday. School.

The a-nnual social was held at the above school on Saturday evening, when there was a very large attend- ance of scholars. The success of the event this year was very materially contributed to by the generosity of Mrs. and Miss Jennings (wife and daughter of the late Superintendent). The former defrayed the cost of presents, and the latter gave a fine tree upon which these were displayed. After recitations and solos had been given by members of the Sunday school, and a number of gramaphone selections by Mr. B. Dimelow, refreshments were served. Then came the distribu- tion of presents and oranges, after which the Doxology was sung, and a highly successful gathering brought to a close.—Messrs. E. Taylor, J. Longworth and R. Halliwell were responsible for the arrangements, and the manner in which they performel their task reflected great credit upon them. - -

On Sunday afternoon the children attending. the above school, to the number of over 300, each received a New Year's gift, consisting of shawls for the girls and scarves for the boys. A short but inspiring address was delivered by the President (Jr. J.Dodds). In the evening a service of song entitled" Little Abe" was rendered 137 the members of the Working- men's Mission Women s Bible Class, under the leader- ship of Mrs. Moore. This week the Committee have been enabled to distribute over 200 gallons of soup and 3001bs. of bread daily to hundreds of poor people. The Committee desire to tender their best thanks to those who have helped. Meat has been given by Councillor Singleton, Messrs. Cross, Fletcher, Ltd., Walsh, Peet, J. and G. Bowcock, Hutchinson, Green- wood, Nelson's Ltd., Tunsiall and R. 0. Tunstall ; vegetables by Messrs. Simpson, Bell, eMcElroy and Sampson.

The Late Mrs. Fred Morrell.

The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Sunday of Mrs. Fred Morrall, 03, Orford-avenae, who passed away on December 31st at the age of thirty-one years. The deceased lady was a very active worker in connection with Cockhedge Mission, and Mr. Morrall is the Sunday School treasurer and secretary of the poor children's treat. Great sympathy is felt with him in his bereavement. The large. attendance of mission workers and friends at the funeral testified to the respect in which the late Mrs. Morrall was held. The Rev. H. Wall officiated and the hymns " Jesu, Lover of my soul" and " It is a thing most wonderful " were sung at the graveside. The chief mourners were Mr. Fred Morrall (widower), Mr. .T. Pearson (father), Mr. Harry Pearson and Mr. Herbert Pearson (brothers), Messrs. G. H. Morrall, C. Morrall and 11. Higham (brothers-in- law), Mr. J. Brandwood (uncle), and Mr. -Hayes. Many floral tributes were placed over the grave, including one from Cockhedge Mission and Sunday School, and one from the Prudential Agents' Union.

At a meeting of the Warrington District of tlo Indepandent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) to be held to-day at the " Admiral Nelson " Lodge,the following resolution is to be submitted: "That this meeting emphatically protests against any form of compulsory national State insurance, which would strike a blow at the principles of individualism and self-help, and pledges itself to resist any such pro- posals as they would be destructive to the best interests of friendly societies. P.S.A. Meetings. A well attended meeting of the Wycliff P.S.A. Society was held on Sunday. Mr. Beawick presided, and wished all present" A. happy aud prosperous New Year." The Rev. John Yonge, the president, gave the address upon " Fight the good fight." He said they all knew something of the difficulties of the present life and he would ask the congregation to fight well, to fight long and he could assure them that if they did so victory would be theirs. He hoped all would fight for the benefit of the P.S A. Their numbers were less because of other meetings which were now held in the town. Still there were many young men who Went nowhere and who would be much better off in their midst. He wished all the members of the society " a happy and useful life." Mr. Yonge made special reference to the death of Mr. G. Thomson and Mr. William Light. The former, he said, was one of the committee and an active worker in the early stages of the P.S.A. Brotherhood. Mr. Light, although not an actual member, often came amongst them, and gave the address from the pulpit with remarkable acceptance. The Secretary moved that a vote of condolence with the bereaved widows and their families be passed and it was carried. Miss Jessie Farrar sang with taste and feeling "The Gift." Mr. Payton presided at the organ. —The weekly meeting of the Warrington Society was held in the old Friars' Green House formerly the rooms of the Young Men's Christian Association. The vice-president (Mr. Brown) presided and an address was delivered by Mr. J. C. Holland who, in taking a retrospect ef the year, gave some very encouraging remarks to the young men present. He advised them to endeavour to build up a noble character both morally and spiritually. Mr. Stanley Garner and Mr. Heywood also took part in the meeting.—Au open meeting of the Buckley- street Society was held in the Buckley-street Church on Sunday. Mrs. Simpson, who presided, gave an encouraging New Year's address. Mr. B. Richardson (Liverpool) was the speaker. Miss Hewitt gave a very impressive rendering of" Lead, kindly Light,' and Mr. Ratcliffe (bass) sang two solos in creditable style. Mr. J. Urruston read the lessons and Miss M. Plinston at the piano.

div.head: SIIOPBREAKEft'S VAIN ARPEAL. –
div.p: A SIIOPBREAKEft'S VAIN ARPEAL. -

At the Cheshire Quarter Sessionie, on Monday, Thomas Glynn, alias Troy (35), tailor, pleaded guilty to breaking and entering the shop of William Taylor Lawson, and stealing four gold bangles at Runcorn, on the 23rd November—Prisoner made a voluble appeal to the Bench to deal leniently with him. lie asserted that he had been certified insane, and when he did anything wrong ho was not conscious of it until afterwards.— The Chairman said prisoner began thieving in the year 1885, and since then he had been convicted thirty times, and had been sent to penal servitude on three occasions. —Prisoner: I have sullered in this life, and when I die I think I will go to heaven. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said it would be idle and a perfect farce to sentence prisoner to less than five years' penal servitude.

div.head: DEATH OF POLICE SUPT. KEIGHLEY.
div.p: DEATH OF POLICE SUPT. KEIGHLEY.

The death was riftbrted on Tuesday, of ex-Super- intendent Keighley, of the Lancashire constabulary force, at his residence, Ribcherter, near Preston. Chief among his exploits was the recovery of the bodies from underneath the hearth in Denham Villa, at Rainhill. He was highly respected by all who knew him in Widnes and South-West Lancashire, and the news of his death has occasioned much regret in Widnes.—Keighley joined the Lancashire County Constabulary Police Force in 1863, and at first worked in the Manchester division. As inspector he was transferred to Welton, and then to Accrington. When the latter town took to itself a borough force, Keighley was sent to Wavertree. Thence he migrated to St. Helens, which scon after followed the example of Accrington. This compelled him again to seek fresh pastures, and he came to Widnes. On December Ist, 1891, he was promoted to the rank of superintendent, and after 13 years of arduous toil in Widnes he retired in 1904. A few days after his retire- ment he was the recipient of a town's testimonial. Shortly after his settlement at Ribchester his health broke down, and for the last two years he had been practo ally an invalid. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tues- day, Mr. T. Baxter presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. J. Spruce, E. Britch, P. Mounfield, P. Booth, C. E. Linaker, J. H. Davies, T. Wright, H. Mawdsley, T. Guest, S. Woodward. W. Harrison, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton, C. Horton, G. Watson, W. M. Morris, P. Collins, A. R Norman, J. Hallows, J. Mynekyme, W. Winstanley, C. E. Linaker, junr., W. Turner, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), T. Cooke, J. Pearson and W. R. de Prez (relieving oflie,ers), and T. D. ltollinson (master). PARLIAMENT AND BE:EFIT SOCIETIES. The Swansea Union forwarded the following resolu- tion for adoption "That in the opinion of this Board, the time has now arrived for some steps to be taken by Parliament to secure to policy holders in Benefit Societies, registered under the Companies Act, the benefits guaranteed by such companies, and that the Government should require a deposit to be made by such companies as is required in the cease of life assurance companies." The letter was referred to the Parliamentary Committee. THE LIGHTING OF THE WORKHOUSE. Mr. Spruce moved that in accordance with the recommendation of the Lighting Committee, applica- tion be made to the Local Government Board to sanction a contract being entered into for the supply and erection of the necessary plant, pipes and fittings, without inviting tenders by advertisment, and that an Incanto Acetelyne Gas Plant be installed at a total cost of £134 7s. 6d., in accordance with the estimate of Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun. Mr. Davies seconded. Mr. Morris said he did not oppose the resolutioa but it was a rather irregular way of expending such a 14rge amount without competitive ten dem Mr. Spruce said a number of- estimates were before the committee and they considered the system they proposed to adopt was the most suitable and also the cheapest. Mr. Mynekyrue : Is there any guarantee given till ' the plant will act ? Mr. Linaker, jun. : Yes. Mr. Morris said he still maintained that tenders should have been invited. For instance, there was the plumbing work which ought to have been tendered for in the usual manner. An estimate had been obtained from one man only. Mr. Linaker, jun. : That is not correct. Mr. Woodward said Mr. Morris was a member of the Lighting Committee and ought td have been present to hear the discussion. He would then have known that every member of the committee was thoroughly con- vinced that the scheme was tbe cheapest and best under the circumstances that they could possibly adopt. There was no inclination to favour anybody. Mr. Morris: Why should— Mr. Liaaker, sen. : I rise to a point of order, Mr. Morris has spoken three or four times on the matter egad we are wasting time. - The Chairman said he understood there were four or five schemes and the one accepted was the cheapest. Mr. Morris: Why should ,special application be made to the Local Government Board to do away with inviting tenders ? The Clerk: It is simply to do away with the necessity of advertising. You have to advertise for anything over £5O unless you get the sanction of the Local Government Board to do away with advertising. If you advertise you will get offers of all descriptions from all over the country—in fact, we have had eight or nine, as it is, from what has appeared in the papers. Mr. Linaker, sen., said the committee considered all the schemes arid prices cud came to the conclusion that the Incanto system was the cheapest and best. Mr. Hallows said he believed the system selected was the cheapest and safest. The resolution was then agreed to. RELIEVING oFFicsit's SALARY.

Mr. Woodward moved that the salary of gr. James Pearson, relieving officer for the Frodsham district, be increased from AUO to £lOO. He said ho believed there was opposition to the proposal in some places, but he was quite convinced that such opposition arose from ignorance of the true facts. When he was appointed Mr. Pearson was given to understand that he would receive the same remuneration as his predecessor and the resolution only meant that the Board's pledge was kept. Mr. Davies seconded, and the resolation was carried unanimously.

, GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES WOMAN VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER. I Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, resumed the inquest at the Widnes Police Station, on Tuesday, touching the death of Elizabeth Houghton (28), wife of a Widnes painter, residing in Edwin-street, who died on December 23rd. Mr. Emma Swindells (4S), residing in Oxford-street, is charged with causing her death.—Ellen Basuett, defendant's daughter, said that her mother lived with ! her up July last year. Witness made arrangements for deceased to see her mother. They met on the 10th at Witness's house, and after a conversa- tion defendant handed to deceased a pint bottle of dark liquid, for which 2s. 3d. was paid. Dralutchinson said he visited deceased on the Pita and 17th of December last. lie found her suffering from peritonitis and in a very exhausted condition. He attended her until the 23rd, when she died. He had made a post-mortem examination and found no external marks of violence, in his opinion the inimediete cause of death was inflammation and blood poisoning set up by internal laceration cud bruises.—Sergeant Davidson gave evidence of arrest, and iu answer to the charge prisoner said : 1 did not do anything with them.— Prisoner made a statement, and said she gave deceased some stud to take, and told her it would du her no harni.—A verdict of " Manslaughter " was returned, land the coroner committed toe defendant iur trial at he next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The enterprise of the Palace management is well exemplified this week in a programme full of novelty and merit Lockhart's elephants, introduced by Captain Taylor, are the chief attraction and their per- formance must surely represent the acme of animal training. At a word from their trainer these intelli- gent creatures do all manner of wonderful things with an ease and alacrity which astonishes as well as pleases the audience. One huge elephant indulges in the strange pastime of standing on its head, while another makes a hobby of cake-walking. " Baby," the humorist of the troupe, has quaint ways which compel laughter. Taking his seat in a restaurant, he rings impatiently for the waiter —another elephant -- and is regaled with" whisky." Having imbibed too freely, " Baby " makes a vain attempt to stagger home, collapses in the roadway and is escorted to the lock-up by an elephant " P.C." " Baby" can also produce wierd and wonderful music by turning the handle of an organ and beating the drum at the same time, and another of his extraordinary accomplishments is to ride a tricycle. The whole troupe join in some effective tableaux and their turn could hardly be excelled The Four Garricks introduce a charming song scena in which the quartette individually and clllectively display vocal talent of a high order and also do some smart dancing. Their show goes with a capital swing and is one of the best of its kind yet seen at the Palace. Les Elgonas present a gymnastic performance which is much above the average, evi- dencing remarkable muscular power as well as agility and daring. Russell Brandow, coloured comedian, makes a speciality of dancing at which he is exceptionally clever, and is rewarded with hearty. rounds of applause. Mollie and Winnie Brooke sing sweetly and dance merrily. The Three Alskarnos figure as Risley comedians, which means that they do acrobatic and tumbling feats in a comical style. They are experts at the business, too, and add not a little to the interest and variety of the programme. John Donald appears in a novel song scena " The Scottish exile's dream " which should appeal powerfully to natives of "The land o' cakes." The prising curtain discloses Donald, in Highland costume, seated at a table on the morrow of the Scottish exile's dinner. Having run over the menu, in which " wee draps" are conspicuous, he begins to soliloquise on the glories of the home land, on the works of the immortal Burns and Scott, and winds up by singing, in a robust voice, a number of Scotch songs, which are illustrated with beautiful views depicted on a screen above the fireplace. J. H. Greener, the singing pit kid, .attired as a rough miner, gives a graphic description in song of the Maypole colliery disaster, together. with a .short recitation expressing gratitude to the King for intro- ducing a decoration for those who perform acts of bravery in the mines. The biograph pictures and the band selections are up to the usual high standard.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. 1-----
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. 1-----
ENGINE OVERTURNED AT EARLESTOWN.

WARRINGTON DRIVERS I,.ZARROW ESCAPE. A serious accident occurred on the London and North-Western Railway, near Earlestown Station on 'Tuesday morning. The engine drawing a lung coal train from flaynuck for Warrington, when about to join the main Warrington line, jumped the rails, and alter running about thirty yards turned turtle. The tender was torn away, and fell across the metals, whilst three coal trucks were derailed. One truck was completely wrecked. The driver of the engine, John lieuwright, Wash-lane, Latchford, Warrington, was able to jump clear though in falling he injured his leg and bead. The fireman was unable to jump away, but by some fortunate chance he was thrown to the uppermost side of the engine as it fell. The wreckage fell completely across the main line from Warrington to Liverpuol,and for the remainder of the morning tad traffic %%AS con- fined to one line, much inconvenience being caused. CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR NEWTON DIVISION.

Viscount Wolnaer, eldest son of the Earl of Se'borne High Commissioner for South Africa, was present at a largely attended meeting of the Excutive Committee of tile Newton Division Conservative Association held on Saturday, Lord Newton presiding. Lord Wolmer delivered an address and also answered a number of questions. A resolution was then unanimously adopted in favour of recommending Lord Wolmer as a suitable candidate for the division at the next election. A general meeting of the members of the Association will be held on Saturday, January 16, at the Newton- le-Willows Town Hall formally to adopt Lord Wolmer. Among those taking part in the discussion on Saturday were Alderman Bennett (Warrington), Alderman Massey (St. Helens), and Lord Gerard. The choice of Lord Wolater will provide a contrast in candidates at the next contest. Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., who in 1906 captured the seat from Colonel Richard Pilkington, is a Labour member. lie is forty years of age, has been a grocer's assistant, a com- mercial traveller, and a lecturer, and is a past presi- dent of the Shop Assistants' Union and the St. llelens Labour Council. The Newton division had returned Tories ever since its creation, but Mr. Seddon, the first Labour candidate, defeated Colonel Pilkington, at the latter's first contest, by a majority of 511-6,134 votes to 5,893. Lord Wolmer was 21 years of age last April. He is a lieutenant in the 3rd Battalion Hampshire Regiment— the family home is in that county. He is the grandson of the Sir Rouniell Palmer who beottin,3 successively Solicitor General, Attorney General, nd Lord Chancel- lor in Liberal Governments previous to the Home Rule split. Lord Wolmer's father, the Earl of Selborne, was First Lord of the Admiralty in the late Conservative Government previJus to his appointment in South Africa in 1935 to succeed Lord Milner as High Com- missioner.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

ST. HELENS TRADESNIAN'S SUDDEN DEATH. The greatest surprise and regret was occasioned at St. Helens, on Monday, by the news of the death of Mr. John Gallie, principal partner of Messrs. Gallia and Co., wine merchants. Mr. Ciallie was thirty-three years of age, and had only been ill a few days. A sudden attack of pneumonia was the cause of death. He leaves a widow and two young children. DEATH OP MR. B. A. DR,OIIGOOLE.

Mr. Bernard Augustin Drorugoole, J.P., dierl at his residence, Sprayhurst, St. Helens, early on ilonday. Mr. Droragoole had been a borough magistrate for the past sixteen years. He was in his ninetieth year, and had resided in St. Helens for over fifty-six years. He was a native of Warrington, but came to St. Helens to manage the Marshall's Cross Pottery, Sutton. In 1853 he setup business as a clothier,%nd was also interested in the establishment of the St. Helens Intelligence," the first local paper. In 1859 Mr. Dromgoole himself started the " St. Helens Newspaper," which he con- ducted in very vigorous fashion. In 1895 Mr. Drom- goole transferred the newspaper and publishing business to his three sons, but retained control of several out- fitting businesses which were established in various parts of the town. In 1900 Mr. Dromgoole had a severe paralytic seizure, but he recovered somewhat, and when he celebrated his eighty-ninth birthday on December 19th last he was in comparatively good health., Mr. Dromgoola has been a member of the Library Com- mittee, and had taken an active part in the government of the town. Ile was a member of the old Board of Commissioners, and at one time he was a member of the Prescot Board of Guardians. He was a prominent member of the Catholic church, and took a great interest in the building of Sacred Heart Church as well as of St. Austin's Giurch, Thatto Heath. Mr. Drom- goole leaves a widow, twelve sous and three daughters.

div.head: DEATH OF nR. 11. R. L.xoEv. A PIONEER, OF THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEAIENT.
div.p: DEATH OF nR. 11. R. L.xoEv. A PIONEER, OF THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEAIENT.

The death took place at St. Helens on Saturday night of Ur. Henry Ratcliffe Lacey, the chairman of the St. Helens Free Library Committee. Mr. Lacey completed his ninety-third year on December 21, lie was born at Wotton-under-Edge, in Gloucestershire, in 1815, th. year of Waterloo. In 1852 he went to St. Helens and began business as a hosier in Church-street. lie did not retire from that business until about 1890. In early days Mr. Lacey took paFt, in the Chartist movement. At one time in his native village there was a great agitation against the payment of Church rates, and Mr. Lacey and his brother, Mr. Newton Lacey, afterwards a schoolmaster in St. Helens, posted every door in the village with bills bearing the words "No Church rates." Hr. Lacey was a Cungregationalist and taught in the -4unday school for over fifty years. lie was an earnest Liberal and Free-trader, and his political hero was John Bright. From his earliest days Mr. Lacey had a great love of licerature, and he did much to advance the Free Librxry movement. The first free public library in St. Helens was opened in the Town Hall on August 20, 1877. Thirty-seven years ago Mr. Lacey. was elected chairman of the Free Libraries Committee, and each successive year he was re-elected,and devoted, himself with great enthusiasm to the work, lie was universally revered, not only by the townspeople, but by the officials arid members of the Library Association to whom his figure had been familiar for many years at i the annual meetings n various parts of the country. ST. HELENS PUBLICAN FINED.

At St. Heleog on Monday, Joseph Haddock, licensee of the Liverpool Arms, Liverpool-road, S. Helens, was charged with selling intoxicating liquors during pro- hibited boars, allowing liquor to be consumed, and allowing gaming on his promises.—Haddock, who was represented by Mr. E. W. Swift, pleaded guilty to allowing gaming to take place on the premises, but denied the offences of selling liquor during prohibited hours.—Thomas Shufliebottom, Cropper's 11111 ; John Disley, ex-policeman, Hardshaw-street ; and Joseph Stamford, Pitt-street, were charged with being on the premises and with aiding and abetting the landlord in permitting gaming.— Chief Constable Ellerington said that on Saturday night, the 26th uIL, Constable Adams and Sergeant Small were on duty in Liverpool-road, and they watched Haddock's house. At 12.39 a.m. they noticed a light in the kitchen, at the rear of the public-house, and heard voices and laughter. Shortly afterwards they heard the landlord go into the bar and draw three corks, and put money into the till. They heard this happen again at 2.15, and after that the sergeant and constable heard the men go out into the yard, where they were talking and laughing for some time. An eight foot wall pre- vented anything being seen, but at four o'clock in the morning Inspector Sisson oarlike on the scene, and he and Constable Adams were assisted over the wall. They maw the landlord and the other three men playing nap, with piles of money in front of them and glasses of beer. When the men had been playing for some time they caught Isight of the policemen. They jumped op, and the land- lord ran out into the yard and told them they would , have to get back over the wall jolly quick. He was ' very angry, and not until the other men remonstrated with him would he let the police go out of the front door.—Mr. Swift said that of the three charges he had expected that only one would have been proceeded with. If the police and magistrates were content to convict only on one information, he would submit to a conviction for gaming. He submitted that according to the Act of 1872 the men, who were guests of the licensee, had not committed any oflence.—Haddock was I fined £5 and costs for permitting gaming, and the other defendants were bound over not to repent the offence.

div.head: ANNUAL TEA MEETINGS.
div.p: ANNUAL TEA MEETINGS.
WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The senior scholars of Wycliffe Sunday school held their annual tea meeting on Thursday evening, when about 170 sat down to tea. Considering the bad state of the weather, the entertainment was well attended by parents and friends of the children, who thraughly enjoyed the varied programme, consisting of solos, choruses, recitations and dialogues. Three classes of girls each in their turn gave action songs, the perform- ances reflecting great credit upon themselves and teachers. Miss Alice Taylor recited in very good style I whilst solos by Mr. J. Poole and Mr. B. 'Ebben were much appreciated. Mr. William Lowe supplied the humorous element. A dialogue given by a class of young girls was well received, the performers evidently having gone to some considerable trouble in studying their various parts. The closing item was an amusing sketch entitled " Quiet Lodgings," in which Messrs. Griffiths, L. Wallington and Jordan displayed a capital knowledge of this particular branch of 'entertainment. During the evening the ltev.J. Yonge presented the prizes to the scholars for regular attendance. PADGATE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual tea meeting in connection with the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday school was held on Thurday evening and, notwithstanding the severe storm which passed over the district shortly before the time fixed for the commencement of the proceedings, over 100 sat down to tea. At a meeting held afterwards Mr. H. E. Roscollor presided. An address was delivered by the Rev. Thomas Gladding who gave a resunid of the work of the church during the year, referring specially to the change of ministers, the recent successful sale of work, and to the gift to the church of a new Communion cloth and pulpit cloth by the family of Mr. John ' Bennett as a thank-offering on the golden wedding of their parents.—An entertainment was provided by the Latchford Glee Party whose items were well received. Miss Lilian Davey rendered two songs very pleasingly, an Mr. William Ford gave some amusing secitations. The school children gave several excellent action songs, for which they had been trained by Miss Lily Ward and Miss Bertha London. All the performers acquitted themselves creditably.—The Sunday school report was read by the Secretary (Mr. Arthur Ward), who recorded an increase af 25 scholars during the year. The number of teachers was 30. The average attendance both of scholars and teachers had increased considerably. Special reference was mhde to the want of accommodation in the schoolroom, and a determined effort will be made to enlarge the premises in the near future,—Votes of thanks were accorded to all who had taken part, on the proposition of Mr. Duckworth, seconded by Mr. William Bennett.

div.head: BOLD STREET WESLEYAN cimacri.
div.p: BOLD STREET WESLEYAN cimacri.

The annual congregational tea meetin7 at Bold-street is generally a success, and last Thursday's gathering was no exception to the rule. About 120 sat down to an enjoyable tea. Trays were given by Mrs. W. Silcock, Mrs. B. J. Guest, Mrs. Toft, Mr. G. Wearer Mrs. J. Fairhurst, Mrs. F. Pandlebury, Mrs. IV. Barlow, Mrs. I. Barlow, Mr. T. B. Carter and Mr. T. Gryme. The ladies of the congregation presided at the tables.

After tea a concert and meeting was held tinier the chairmanship of the Rev. Thomas Miller, supported on the platform by the superindendent of the Sunday School,Mr. J. C. llolland and Mr. W. Dean. The CHAIRMAN in opening the proceedings said that that was a congregational tea arranged by the congrega- tion and the Sunday school. He hoped that as a congregation and as a Sunday school they would have a prosperous new year. He hoped there would be nothing to mar the peace of the church and that everything that made for the strengthening of it might find a place in the church life. They had to record the death of several friends including Miss Jones, Mr. Pattison and several others. The only influence that these lives could have upon them was by resolutely resolving to follow in their late friends' footsteps as they followed in Christ's.So:uo people spoke of "poor old Bold-street." Well, "poor old Bold-street" was not poor, and if Bold-street was old it had only gained wisdom in its years. (Applause.) They had a magnificent opportunity, and they ought to adapt themselves to the times in which they were living, by trying to understand some of the things the people needed. He believed there was nothing to hinder Bold-street being full. Taere was nothing to hinder them from having a ! greater number in the church membership. The church existed not to pay its way, because if it only did that, the object of the church was accomplished and it ought to be burnt down to-day. There was no church which existed simply for the reason of paying its way. It only existed for the good it could do, They wanted to get the people into a reel living fellthcship with Jesus Christ. Ills judgment was, that if they would only keep their eyes open, forget everything of the past and resolve to consecrate themselves to Jesus Christ their church would be a great blessing in the neighbourhood, and he trusted that they themselves ! would be blessed ie the new year. He recommended that in 1909 they did the work of 1939 and not the work of 1815 or 1855. (Applause.) Mr. J. C. IiomAND (Society Steward) said that he did not think they need regret anything as far as their work was concerned in 80ld-street. lie v..zs delighted to see that during the year the chapel and Sunday school had gathered in many God-fearing men and women. (Applause.) Mr. E. PIANSTON (secretary to Sunday School Com- mittee) sub.uitted his report. This was Mr. Pr,rxsToN's first anneal report, andshe ! rejoiced in the harmony and concord of the past year's werk, lie paid eloquent testimony to the servies of their friend and pastor, the Rev. Thomas Hiller, and to the Saturday night Concert Committee, who were achieving the end they had in view in filling the chapel. The work of the Sunday school had been fairly satisfactory considering the dearth of teachers. The average morning attendance was 91 scholars and 8 teachers ; afternoon, 171 scholars and 17 teachers including the officials. Conduct had been good, and between 70 and SO scholars have qualified for prizes. The socretary made a pasiiag reference to the satisfactory resuscitation of the defunct Band c• Hope, and to the efficiency of other school offices. Reference was also made t 5 the loss caused by the death of Mr. F. Light, and the report concluded with an appeal for greater sympathy and support in the work of the Sunday school from every member of the con4re,a tion, so that the year just entered upon might be the happiest on record in the history of the school. Mr. \V. DEAN said it was no good being miserable and he would not give a fig for a man who had a long face. One thing that Christianity did was that it gave a joy in life. The SUPERINTENDENT and Mr. E. LUNT (a former secretary of the Sunday school), also spoke. The excellent programme which was submitted included the following :—Miss E. Taylor. " Kathleen Mavourneen "; Mrs. E. A. S orders, " Home, sweet home "arid "Annie Laurie " ; Mr. Ratter, cornet solo ; Mr. Warburton, tenor solo ; Mr. E. A. Sanders, humorist.
A hearty vote of thanks was itc;,•orded to the artistes.

div.head: LATE MR. WILLIAM LIGHT.
div.p: THE LATE MR. WILLIAM LIGHT.

Many readers of' Examiner " will learn with regret the death of Mr. William Light, which occurred at his residence, Wellfield-street, on 31st December. Deceased who was bora at atkengates, Salop, was 66 years of ago at the time of his death. At the age of 13 he com- menced local preaching, and continued in this Christian work until he came to Warrington in 1831, where he soon made many friends. Arrived at Warrington he joined the ranks of the Wesleyan local preachers and served loyally for 27 years, completing a service of 43 years on the plan. He was a society class leader for 25 years at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. He was employed at Sankey Wire Hills, where he enjoyed the confidence of his masters and fellow workmen, until four years ago, when a paralytic stroke forced him to give tip his occupation. However, he was able to get about until November of last year, when he fell a victim to enteric fever. Still hopes were entertained that he would be restored, but congestion of the lungs and syncope ensued and the result proved fatal. Mr. Light was a Liberal in politics and took an intelligence interest in the doings of his party, but his poor health in recent years prevented him from actively associating himself with them. He leaves a widow and eight children.

The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. Thomas Miller, in Bowey-road Wesleyan Church, at one o'clock on Sunday last, and was largely attended. During the service the rev, gentleman expressed on behalf of those present their sympathy and then prayers for the family which had been bereaved. Their brother who had departed was a good witness of the Lord. There was no need why they should be serious; because he had entered into a now life. The labourers work was over ; the work was finished ; the work which he had been engaged in for many years, in pro- claiming Jesus Christ was finished. He had lived a Christian life and his message from the pulpit was one of joy to the Christian worshipper. The brethren who were engaged in the large and arduous task of local preaching, were only different to the ministers, because they had not the same opportunities of proclaiming the Gospel. Mr. Light's acceptability as a preacher manifested some study ; and he was always sincere in his work. They would like to bear witness to his virtues. lie preached his first sermon in Lilleshall, Shropshire, in a little cottage. At that time he was a member of one of the sister bodies of methodisrn who were becoming closer and closer, lie believed that before the end came he (Ir. Light) was imagining him- self preaching and giving out the hymms he so much loved. They prayed that front his life they would gain some inspriation ; and from his faith they would be helped to bear the suffering. After the service the local preachers and friends lined up in front of the hearse and formed a procession to the cemetery. The Rev. E. I3lansham Keeling conducted the last rites at the graveside and gathered around were representatives of all the Nonconformist bodies in the town.
The funeral arrangements were in the hands of Messrs. G. and J. Weaver.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Emmanuel Church. On Wednesday last at 8 o'clock the flrst of a series of Bible study classes was held in the Institute of the above Church. The object of the classes is to promote the spiritual growth of Christians in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. With. this object in view the Rev. F. Vaughan is arranging a course of study calculated to help those who are earnestly striving to live as Christians in daily life. On Wednesday evening there was a good attendance and the subject studied," Oar Divine Companion," was so unfolded by Mr. Vaughan that those present are likely to find it helpful for many days to come. Bold-street Wesleyan Church. On Sunday evening in place of the usual evangelistic service in the schoolroom, and after meeting was held in the church immediately following the ordinary service. It was conducted by the Rev. T. Miller, and proved helping and inspiring. It took the form of a "prayer—praise, and testimony meeting," in which the Rev. 'I. Miller, Mr. W. Gleave, Ur. J. Wallace (recently from the Wigan Mission). Mr. J. C, Holland, and Mr. Dean took part.—Mr. Edwards, who has just arrived from Elamilton, Canada, on a visit to his old home and church, told of some good work going on in his church across the'seas, and expressed the feelings of brother- hood existing between Canadian and British Methodism. He was sorry to miss such old faces as good old Dr. Starkey Smith, Mr. Richardson and many others ; yet he rejoiced in the fact that they had each gone to receive the reward laid up for the faithful.

St. Peter's Church. The Rev. B. Percival, vicar of St. Peter's Church, entered upon the 17th year of his ministry there on Sunday, and in the evening he preached a special sermon, taking as his text the motto for the year, 11. Cor. v. 14," Tho love of Christ constraineth us." The chief movements in England were Socialism and that relating to women. There was a great desire to improve our industrial conditions. The militant Socialists were serving the cause of the humble wage- earner very badly, and there was a danger of reaction, while the militant suffragettes were serving the cause of their sex equally badly. The supreme force that moulded character was what men believed concerning things unseen, and the deepest problems of the time were neither political nor industrial, but religious. The things that were not seen were the real things. Moses endured as seeing Him who was invisible. People in these days said there was a vast amount of indifference in regard to religion, and that there was a vast amount of scepticism, but he contended that there never was an age in which religion interested men more than it did now.

The Work In St. James's Parish. St. James's Magazine says :—We have much to be thankful for in our parish when we attempt to review the past year. !t is a great thing to have been able to secure a second assistant curate. It had long been evident that a parish the size of ours should have at least three clergy and at last we have made up the number. Our bazaar too was distinctly encouraging. The good feeling and readiness to help which was so characteristic of the unclertakiug was very pleasant, and a substantial sum of money was raised. As you know, half the money forms the nucleus of a new mission church fund. Some good people are under the impression that we shall begin to build our new church almost itnmediately. But, unfortunately, we cannot,for we shall require more thousands of pounds than at present we have hundreds. We have made n start to help our- selves, which is something. The next step is to lay the case of our poor pariah before the consideration of generous Churchpeople who may be interested in our work ha this place and we hope for their substantial support. Everyone will be glad to know that the year past has been a very prosperous one at St. Hilda's. Its congregation is steadily growing. Sunday school is increasing in numbers and usefulness, and its Church- yard—if the ground surrounding the Mission may be so termed—has been transformed into a highly orna- mental garden. At St. James's the new choir vestry is in course of construction an I will shortly be ready for use. The screens at the west end of the church seem likely to cost more than we thought, and so we have not finally decided what course to adopt, However screens of some sort will be placed in the archways which now admit such a large amount of draught, and we shall welcome their arrival. Wycliffe Church. , The opening of the New Year was fittingly observed at Wycliffe Congregational Church, last Sunday. In the morning a young people's service was held, when the preacher was the Rev.A.A.Lee of Bootle,who gave a very encouraging address. At the close of the service, the annual presentation of i-,-.17cF.; tO tb.S' 1-.3embere of tbo Pastor's cateehiateeet elass took phoe. In the evening the Rev. J. Yonge occupied the pulpit, and preached a powerful sermon on the ‘Vscliffe motto for 1909. "Be strong and work, for I am with thee," (Haggai ii. 4 v.) After dwelling upon the personal use of the New Year motto, the rev. gentleman said that he desired also to invite them to accept the motto as a precept and encouragement to their united continual endeavour to make that church in every respect, efficient and success- ful. In the test, God was reminding them that the House of God and the service of God could not be either built or fulfilled with- out hands, without personal labour, without united and continual endeavour. So there was evident lesson in their motto for their Church life. They had not (at least there at Wycliffe) to rise and build, although there was a call coming to them even of that kind within their own community. But the call was loud and urgent for thorn to arise and co-operate for the true up-building of the spiritual Church. It would be a good day for Wycliffe when its people realized more fully how its corporate prosperity depended upon the devotion, industry, sacrifice of each individual member. net was true of all the various phases of their church life and work. He (Mr. Yonge) wished that any word of his, that New Year's Sunday, could evoke a sense of that duty to the Church and the Master which every person belonging to them should feel. They wanted that valuable, powerful sentiment indispensable to the true success of any corporate institution which the French people described as "esprit de corps." They wanted the feeling of individual loyalty to the whole spiritual society to which they belonged. Golborne-street Baptist Church. On Sunday morning the Rev. R. E. Letheren took for his text "Without were fightings, within were fears a nevertheless God. . . ." 2 Cor. vii., 5, 6. He said that the Christian life was sometimes thought of as if it were a sort of spiritual Lotus Land, a land where it was always afternoon. But to the Apostle life was strife. It was true that the great words of the Gospel were peace, joy, rest ; but the peace was that which came from victories won ; the joy of that tranformed sorrow, the rest that of perfected motion and not stagnation. The Christian man and the church were to expect conflict. There was fighting without—against sin, ignorance, misunderstanding, opposition, and fears within—on account of timidity, past failures, lukewarm- ness. Nevertheless God ! His presence and power, His goodness in the past, His promises for the future, inspire us with confidence and make us more than conquerors. At the Brotherhood Meeting in the after- noon Mr. Letlaeren gave an address on 1. Cor. xvi., 13-11. He might have called it he said, a" Fived lined Whip for the New Year." The notes of the message were Watchfulness, against temptation and for oppor- tunities of service. Steadfastness in the faith, faith in God and faith in life. Manliness in thought and feeling, Strength of purpose. Love as energy of life. In the evening the subject was taken from Exodu s xiv., 15, "Go Forward." The passage illustrated three forces that made for progress. There was that behind which drove them forward ; that within which determined them to go forward. Canaan before which drew them forward. Was tkere not something in their own past which drove them forward ? Influences towards plod that had grown weaker • evil habits that had grown stronger ? The waning of their Christian ideals, their growing indifference to the gospel appeal should from the danger of them 'drive them forward. Was there with a New Year a determination to go forward ? The promises of Christ drew them forward. With several apt illustrations Mr. Letheren then emphasised the appeal. Fix well thy centre first. Go from the Cross. Do not stand always on the point of going forward and yet remain where you are. Go with a hoe in your hand to work in Christ's vineyard and not only eat the grapes. Go forwatd and pray as you go. And pay as you go. See that ye fall not out by the way. Go on unto perfection, keep the goal before you. During the service Mrs. Peart very beautifully rendered "The Gentle Shepherd."
THE MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL DISTRICT' BANKING COMPANY LIMITED.

The following is the report of the directors of the above bank, to be submitted to n. meeting of share- holders on Friday next, at the head office of the company in Manchester.—The directors have to repoe6 that the gross profit for the half-year ending 31st December last, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, is £295,558 4s. 4d. to which has to be added the amount brought forward from 30th June last, viz.: £52,613 12s. 2d,; total £348,171 16s. 6d. From thissurn the following deductions have to be made:—Total expenses at the head office, London office, and branches, incladiug salaries, stationery, income tax, &c., £113,781} us. 4d., leaving a net profit of £234,382 ss. 2d. The directors recommend the declaration of a dividend of 21s. per share, which will take £165,900 leaving a balance of £68,482 ss. 2d. Of this it is pro- posed to carry to the reserve fund £lO,OOO, to pension fund £5,000, and to next account £53,482 ss. 2d. The reserve fund, with the above addition, will amount to £1,705,000. The directors regret to intimate that Mr. John Sanderson, for many years a director of the Lancaster Bank, and elected a director of this Bad( in January, 1908, died on the 30th December. The term of office of the following directors will expire on the 15th instant, viz., Messrs. John Frederick Knott, John Parks, Edward Partington, Peter Jaffrey Ramsay. They are eligible and are recommended for re-election.
EDWARD DONNER, Chairman. Manchester, 6th January, 1909.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

Football was tame in the extreme last Saturday at Wilderspool, and it is a fact that the two home games with Welsh clubs have been the least interest- ing of the season. The chief reas'm seems to be that the issue was never in doubt from the commence- ment, though both Merthyr and Ebbw Vale pushed Warrington hard. Personally I think that the exceedingly poor foothill of the Warrington men in these two games has had a lot to do with their unattractiveness. There seemed to be no life about the hoinesfers on Saturday. Probably the hard gams of the previous day had something to do with the apathy shown, but really the men were not excited by the c ntest with Ebbw Vale.

Yet the Valians did their best to make things • inter- esting. They played clever and dashing football all through the first half and made the home lot appear quite second-rate. Ebbw Vale opened the scoring. and it took Wartington all their time to ~.equalise before the interval. On resuming, the locals displayed more determination, and while their methods lacked the usual polish they proved too strong for the lighter men opposed to them. Eight more points were added to Warrington's score and they wen comfoitably won by 113.

• The absence of Taylor and Brooks upset the com- bination of the home side, whose passing was not really equal to that of the visitors. The Welshmen have improved since their last visit to Warrington,and with a little more weight in the pack they would make a formidable team. Dai Davies, the old War- rington half-back, wears tematkably well and his display at full back for the Valians was consistently good. I notice that he is also reserve for the Welsh League team against the Kangaroos.

Two matches were played on Monday which affected clubs with an interest in the first four of the League. Runcorn spoiled their chances to a serious extent by going down at Barrow 113. This was a rather surprising win for the Furness men, and while it would be very welcome to them, it would be rather a bitter pill for the Linnets. Oldham journeyed to Swititte where their usual luck did not desert them. They won by 5 points to 2 after having bad all the worst of the game The Blues missed some of the. simplest chances to score through over-eagernese—
The League table up to date is as follows: For A gs t. Per

Warrington have a stiff programme to get through before the end of February. To-day they visit Hull, then Wakefield come to Warrington. After this Warrington visit St. Helens, Wakefield, Oldham and lialifax in succession. If the Wirepullers can average a point a match from these six engagements they should finish the season in good company, for every League match in March and April can be won.

Warringtoa will make the long journey t ) Hull to-day with fair prospects of success. They have uenerally given a god acconnt a themselves at the Boulevard, and on more than one occasion they have won The very erratic form of the Hull men suggests that Warrington's steadiness On the defence and strong attacking power may pull them through. Yet it has to be recognized that on their day Hull can play as fine a game as any team. With full strength available Warrington should have a very good chance. lam glad a change has been made in the forwards, for the latter have been playing.indifferently of late and the use of the spur was necessary. '
The selected team is Tilley, full bsck ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Treharne, three-quarters ; Jenkins an.l Tiro )Ic., half hacks; Thomas, O'Neill, Dowell, Chesters, Belton and Naylor, forwards.

The " A " team will he at home to Leigh Shamrocks, and will have the following strong side out, Mclntyre, full back; Lawlor, Jordan, Cartwright and Bradshaw, three-quarters ; Lloyd and .Lees, half backs; Harmer, Gibb 9, Forster, Bradshaw, Fairhurst and Harrison, forwards.

The Warrington Committee mean to strengthen the team for the N. U. Cup-ties if possible, and they are at present in negotition for one of the Wallabies' backs. The capttire will create a sensation if it comes off. It needs only half an eye to see that injury to either of the present centres will cripple the Warrington team, at:d there is no one class enough to fill the vacancy. Another forward or tvo are essential in my view, for if anything the pick lacks weight. If F. Jenkins and Shugars can be persuaded to turn out again the difficulty will be solved.
To.day the Wallabies meet the ehlsen of England at Blackheath, and there will be one or two keenly iuterented Warri3gtonians making a study of form.

div.head: WORKERS' THRIFT.
div.p: WORKERS' THRIFT.
Huge Savings and How to Protect Them

A rims of interesting detail concerning the thrift or the masses is contained in the report of the Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies, issired on Wednesday. A general view of the present position of tho various thrift organisations now in existence in Great Britain and Ireland and the* funds may be obtained from the following summary. The particulars of Friendly Societies are for the year 1905, and of the remaining closers for 1906, and the membership and the bank depositors with the huge sums represented afford a striking object-lesson : Sccieties, Members. Funds. Building 616,729 £7125,8426 Friendly 1,4(109.869
. . Co-operative e2,467,806 52,960,807 Trade Unioni Workmen's Compensation ... 103,444 Labour Loan 33,500 Certified and P.O. Depositors. Deposits. Savings Bank 12,159,133 242,651,331
Grand Total

With regard to ordinary friendly societies and those with branches alone (the membership of which, at the end of 1905 numbered 5,899,918), the curious statement is made that the principal increase in membership since 1893 occurred in persons under 16 years of age.. Of the total number, 256,479, or only 4•3 per cent. were over 65. Female membership, too, ehoNsed little advance.

As regards old age pay and annuities, the information to be gathered from the returns is meagre. Relatively few societies make the provision as apart from perman- ent sickness or invalidity pay, and in the aggregate the amount paid during the year was under £170,000. Another fact brought out in the report is that during the period 1899-1905 investments of the societies in land, buildings and mortgages have increased from £250.2 per £l,OOO to £5971. This development is interesting in view of the proposed Taxation of Land Values, and its incidence. With regard to the need of a prompt and efficient audit, Mr. Stuart, Sim is emphatic. lie rays that the attention of his ofrce is frequently drawn, too late, to losscs from defalcations, misappropriations, and to improper investments of the funds—three causes which, peibaps, constitute the greatest dangers to which societies ane subject. "While a more searching audit may not give entii e immunity from such unfortunate experiences, it will reduce the possibilities of losses of this nature to a minimum, and the members may well consider the expenditure incurred for auditors' fees as partaking of the nature of a premium of insurance for the proper administration of the funds."
The words of ‘Villiam \Vat= might have been written by the pen of the Editor of "The Dawn" Friend call me what you will ; no jot care I. I that stall stand for England till I die, *

The England from whose side I have not swerved ; The immortsl Bugland whom T, too, have served, Accounting her till living lands above, In, Justice, and in Mercy, and in Love. The imperial idea is ever passionately strong, and the Alderman is prepared to adopt any policy which he conceives to be right for binding with stronger ties the mother country to her c)lonies. Arpin I would borrow from Watson:s words to express what I conceive to be Alderman Bennett's feeling towards the Empire.

Whom should I trust if not my kin? And whom Account so near in natural bonds as these, Barn of my tnother England's mighty womb, Nursed on my mother England's mighty knees, And lull'd as I was lull'd, in glory and in gloom, With cradle song of her-protecting sets?

But it would be a mistake to convey the idea that his fervour is exhausted by its vision outward. He saes very clearly that the heart of the Empire must be sound, that an imperial race cannot be evolved out of squalor, p3verty, slutnt,.and drunkenness, and so again borrowing from Watson I would express lfr. Bennett's thought in the following:

Your savage deserts howling near, Your wastes of ignorance, vice, and shame, Is there no room for victories here, No field for deeds of fa:ue? Arise and conquer while ye can The foe that in your midst resides, And build withia the mind of man The Empire that abides. Or to put the matt3r in his own words " Loving England with a passi,mate devotion almost from our very cradle, as we grew hi years, we saw the dear old land the prey to parties which alternAtely mismanaged her affairs, with wealth beyond the dreams of avarice, yet miserably poor, absorbed in low ideals, boasting of a Christianity she loudly preached, but seldom practised ; her soft green bosom scarred with all the horrors of the factory system ; her rivers fouled, her skies polluted; her rich men living idle and lurarious lives, her poor consenting to their pigdotn if they had ennugh to pay to see the weekly footbdl mitch or dronn their sorrows in a pint of beer.'

I said at the beginning that Aft.. amlnett's apparent inconsistency was a puzzle to his plitic d friends,wha never quite know when they have hiat L. is true that ' his sytupaties and support frequently alternate from the actions of one p triy to those of the other, but this arises from the breadth and variety of his sympathies and the possession of ideals to.) seldom found in con- junction. If I might venture a word of advice to our friend I would say : Keep yourself separate from all parties, confine yourself in the main to your proper role as seer, poet, and reformer, leaving the more practical questions to minds of lower range and possibly more logical aptitude. You have a messago and a mission to yoar tosns.nan of ail p trties and of none, but it is one which necessarily places you aloof from all, and in a sense aitove all. I do not want to imply that the Alderman is merely a theorist and is deficient itt practical ability. This is not so, his training and surroundings have compelled him ever and again to hew wood and draw water, but his natural place is with those who see visions and dream dreams ; here he breathes his native air and draws his inspiration from above. And in an age that is stamped with utilitaraniam we can ill afford to have ibe prophet cloud his vision by the study of such things as the effect of imports upon exports. The prophet loses his power, strength, and influence, when his lays aside his mantle and turns again to the plough. C. E. P.

div.head: Fall Accelerates Consumptlon.
div.p: Fall Accelerates Consumptlon.

Mr. Corontx Brighouse held an inquest at the Police SOtion on Tuesday, touching the death of Thomas Magrath (40), 61, Found, y-street, Warrington. The evidence showed that Magrath left the 8 .30 train from Manchester, and was going down the Central Stition steps into the street when lie fell. ITe was in a drunken condition. First aid was rendered, and deceased was afterwards conveyed to the Infirmary. Dr. Russell, house surgeon,at the Infirmary, stated that the immediate cause of death was consumption, but the fall had accelerated it. Mr. J. Ramage, who represented the Railway Company, said their had not been any accident on thee steps for about fivei years to his knowledge. Mr. Da rbyshi`re, the stationina6ter, said be did not know of any similar accident during the tithe he had been connected with the station.—The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."
WARRINGTON RAILWAY THEFTS.
Smart Sentences

The Warrington Police Court on Tuesday presented the appearance of a general dealer's shop, a varied assortment of goods including leather, hats, gloves, cheese, pickles, silk gause, wearing Apparel, and numer- ous tins of fruit, toffee, and blacking being piled on the solicitors' benches. The goods were alleged to have been stolen from railway transit vans at the Lon:Ion and North-Western Ruilway Siding at Froghall. John Morton, Iviredrawer, Monks-street •, Thomas Walton, engine-driver, Monks-street; and Edvin Hamer, labourer, Oaskell-street, were brought before the magistrates, on remand, charged as follows : Walton and Morton, on December 20th, stealing and receiving from a van in transit a bale of leather value .610, the property of the Railway Company ; further with stealing and receiving from a van in transit on December 19th, one cheese and 32 packets of jelly, valued at .£1 10s. 01., the property of the Railway Com- pany ; farther with stealing and receiving from a van in transit 154 yards of silk gauze, value £2; IValton and Hamer, charged with stealing from a van in transit a quantity of men's and boys' clothing, value £l2, on October 2nd, the property of the Railway Company. Mr. A. Eddy (solicitor) appeared on behalf of the L. & N.-W. Railway Company, and Mr. T. S. Steel -epresented the prisoner Walton.—All three prisoners pleaded guilty to the charges. Mr. Eddy said there had been a series of systematic robberies from that company's siding, extending over a period of six months. The property which was in court had been reccerered from the house of the prisoner ' Walton. Early on Sunday morning, December 20th, the prisoner Morton was seen to break into a van which was standing in the Froghall siding of the London and North-Western Railway. Another man was with him but he succeeded in getting away. Morton also tried to escape, but after a chase he was caught. The prisoner Walton's house was then visited, and he was found to be fully dressed and also had muddy boots, this being at 4 o'clock in the morning. The house was searched and the stolen goods were found. Some of the goods had not yet been recovered and in all probability would never be found, having been disposed I of by the prisoners who reaped the benefit of the trans- action.. The prisoner Walton had been in the 'employ I of the railway for something like 37 years as an engine- driver, but was discharged for drunkenness Walton was evidently the ringleader, because he had intimate knowledge of the workings of the railway compauy. Prisoners took the goods to be stolen out of a transit waggon and placed them into a waggon that was likely to stay in the siding for a long period, and afterwards removing them at their leisure. The prisoner Hamer g•ho was arrested on information given by one of the prisoners was wearing part of a suit. of clothes which formed one of the subjects of the charges against him. Regarding Morton, Mr. Eddy stated that he had been living in the town for a year. He was not living with his wife who was a respectable women, and he did not appear to help her in any way. He had been living with the prisoner Wilton, in Monk-street. Mr. Steel on behalf of the prisoner Walton, said that he had been in the employ of the railway company for 37 years as an engiue-driver but was discharged for an alleged lapse of duty. From the moment of his dis- charge from the Company he had lost all ambition and self-respect and appeared to have got into bad ways. He had bean unable to got suitable employment and had apparently committed the robberies from desperation. Previous to his discharge he had been of very good character. He had made no attempt to dispose of the goods, which were found in a shed at the back of the house. it was also %%Talton who helped the police in the arrest of Hamer, fie had suffered great remorse while in prison for the 16 (Ilya. Ile had been left, in solitary conflaernent and had undergone great punishment. He (Hr. Steel) asked the megistrates not for the sake of the prisoner, but for his wife and family, who held respectable positions, to deal as leniently as possible with the case. . _ - -
Flamer, in answer t•-) the chirp, stated that he had had a drop of drink and got into Walton's company,and that but for him ho would n have been tn the dock.

The tn-agistrates discussed the c,ise in private. and on rotArning the chairman (N 1 r. H. Roberts) stated that their decision WAS that Walton be sentenced to nine months' itnprisontnent w ith hard labour, and Morton and Hamer to six months with hard labour each.

CAM, TIERTZ AND THE SMALL BOY.
Cnel Hertz, the clever conjuror, once had a droll experience, to. which he refers as his fadure.

It came one night during the time-honoured trick of squeezing a half-crown that has been marked into an orange, and then producing the coin fi•om the pocket of some person in he audience. He squeezed the coin in, and hcn picking out a small boy, who sat on a far off seat, he called out : " Now my young friend, I think you will find I have passed the Marked coin into your left hand trousers pocket." The lad fumbled slowly in his pockets, and brought out a shilling, two sixpences, and four pennies. • " That's not , the half-crown," said. the conjurer, who began to feel uneasy. • No sir." said the boy, " I was so thirsty that I took your half-crown to the bar as I .came in and had a bottle of gingerbeer." Carl Hertz has now learnt wisdom, and no longer has Jbusiness dealings with small boys. H. DINGLEY.

Ah well do I recall how, in the happy olden days, I sat beside the nursery fire and saw the hickory blaze; While I heard the wind without, and the splash- ing of the rain, And the broad magnolias tapping at the drip- ping window-pane, When Mammy, rocking slowly, with the baby on
her knee; Told many a _wondrous story—" jus' ez true ez _ .

SUSAN ARCHER WEISS. A YOUNG 'FINANCIER.

Nellie, whose grandfather began life as a cabin-boy and ended as a millionaire, was paid by her mother a penny a dozen for pins picked up from the carpet, to keep the baby from getting them. "Nurse," said Nellie, as her stock of pennies increased, "do you know what I ant going to do when I have sixpence ? " " No miss."
"I am going to buy a paper of pins and scatter them over the floor, and then pick them up," replied the five-year-old financier.

_ - THE FLAG OF ENGLAND. Unfurl the Flag of England, • And fling it to the breeze; Beloved by British hearts at home, And those beyond the seas; The symbol, as in ages gone, Of reverence for the right, That leads men ever on and on Through liberty to light. Its folds to all of friendship speak, Of enmity to none ; Protection for the wronged and weak Wherever shines the sun ; And when the Union Jack Is seen - Rippling o'er wave or wind, Alen hail it, for its tidings moan Peace unto all mankind. God guard the Flag of England, The Empire, and the Throne, And sister nations far away In every sea and zone! And When at -freshening dawn it flies Anew beneath the sky, Vow We once more, should need arise, To strike for it, and die. V. HOLT.
