For further particulars see "Post Office Guide," at any Vost Office. POSTAGE STAMPS._ _
Books containing 12 penny and 23 halfpenny stamps are now on sale at each post office. Price 2s.
INLAND CORRESPONDENCE.

The term " Inland Correspondence" means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes: (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. LErrca POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows : Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... id. For every additional 2 0z5.... id. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth.

POST-CARDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 incites in width, or be less than 3t inches in length by 2t inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and finch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter.

~• HALFPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, Ike. not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is 1. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the post like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. • The-rates of postage-on parcels areas follows: Fora pprcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 ” exceeding 1 113.. If 2 lb. 0 4 „ 2 lb. If 3 lb. 0 5 t f ff If 3 lb. Of 5 lb. 0 6 it If 5 lb. If 7 lb. 0 7 fl tt 7 lb. ), 8 lb. 0 8 9 f tt 8 lb. ff 9 lb. 0 9 ff ft 9 lb. 2IP 10 lb. 010 9, t, 10 lb. It 11 lb. 011 No parcel may exceed 111 b. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel in:— Greatestlength... ... ... ... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 It. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. 61n. in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. 6in. round its thickest pare; a short parcel may be thicker; thus, if it measure no more than 3ft. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part._ .

The postage on a parcel must be prepaa. Mark each parcel" Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL).

Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.)

The postal authorities cannot issues single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d. ; £3,.3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, lOd. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions.

div.head: MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.)
div.p: MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.)

The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, ad. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 64. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enabled money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad.

div.head: POSTAL ORDERS.
div.p: POSTAL ORDERS.

These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by Gd., from Gd. to RI. Is. The poundage fees are :—id. up to 2s. Gd.; Id. up to 158.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always 1M in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as Is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- maater-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND).

The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a.telegram is a minimum amount of 6(1., which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each 'extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from kt head telegraph office, but if from a sub7office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word: The cost of a reply may be wend& 'Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the .nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is 21 Is.

TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the hank on behalf of children under 'seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and thi,s may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed.at the rate of 2. per cent. Any amount up to and including £t may he withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank bocik. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on tho anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK IfINE. CHARGES.

Warrington Still Winning The Ebbw Vale men were the visitors to Warrington on Saturday, and they gave the homesters a very good game. It was expected that Warrington would have an easy victory,but the visitors proved theii claim to be ona of the best League teams in Wales and showed smart football. Neither side was quite at full strength, the visitors being without Foley, their international for- ward, and Warrington were short of Brooks and Taylor. Fine weather prevailed, and the ground was in capital order. _ The attendance was about 4,000.. .Teams :

--Warrington--Tilley, back; Fish, Dicl enson, Cart- wright and Treharne, three-quirter hacks; Lloyd and Jenkins, half hacks; Dowell, Neill, Thomas, A. E. Boardman, P. Boardman, and Chesters, forwards. Ebbw Vale—Dai Davies, back ; Jenkins, H. Smith, Iliggins and Llewellin, three-quarter hacks; Harvey and Tiiolllab ; Saunders, Hutchings, Monks, Mayle, Leah and Brown forwards. Referee, Mr. E. H. Smirk, Wigan. Touch judges, Messrs. R. Jones, Widnes, and W. Gregory, Runcorn. Warrington started the game. but showed poor form at the commencement. Ebbw Vale were very aggressive, and fine individual runs by Smith and Jenkins caused Warrington aniiety. Eventually Tilley, Dickinson, and Lloyd in turn eased the pressure, and Davies' charge was reached. Effective passing by Higgins and Llewellyn led up to Thomas dodging over from a pack near the line, Jenkins failing at the place. Warrington effected a fine rally, and eventually after good combina- tion Treharne• completed a try from Cartwright's pass. At half-time the score was one try each.

Turning round the bore forwards speedily asserted themselves, and after Dickinson end Trehearne had been pulled up at the corner, Cheaters went over from a forward rush. Warrington still forced matters and Lloyd dodged over from a pack, for Fish to add the goal. Ebbw Vale attacked in the closing stages, and both Jenkins and Llewellyn were pulled up in turn near the line, after brilliant rur.s. Result :—Warrington, 1 goal 3 tries (11 points), Ebb Vale 1 try (3 poiats).
The Examiner, Saturday, January 9, 1909.

div.head: ROCHDALE IIORNETS v. WIDNES.
div.p: ROCHDALE IIORNETS v. WIDNES.

Four thousand spectators witnessed this match at Rochdale. The Hornets attacked, and good play by Farrar and Baxter placed them in a favourable position. Baxter whipped the ball out to English, who was left with a clear field, but be missed the ball, and a flee chance was lost. Farrar next got in a good kick. Following up speedily he charged down Jones's kick, and catching the ball on the bounce opened the score for the Hornets. Robinson failed at the goal kick. There was no further score before the interval.

In the second half the fog became so thick that it was impossible to follow the movements of the players, but the referee did not think fit to stop the match. ‘Vidnes attacked, but could not got over, and at the other end Turner scored an unconverted try. The match was stopped ten minutes before time. Result :—Rochdale Hornets 2 tries (6 points), Widnes nil.

div.head: PRICE OF SOAP.'
div.p: THE PRICE OF SOAP.'

Messrs. lever Bros. have issued circulars to their customers announcing a reduction of Id. per pound in the price of their soaps. This, it is explained, is due to the fact that during the last 18 months tallows and oils used in laundry soap making have fallen in price, viz.: tallows from £2 10s. to £3 and oils from 28 to .29 a ton. Whatever the price 18 months ago, it is added, the price to-day should be about Ad. per pound' less, and their prices are reduced accordingly from the Ist inst.

Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., interview with reference to the above announcement, stated that the paragraph contained a somewhat belated reference to reductions in the prices of tallows and oils used in the manufacture of household soaps, the inference intended to be conveyed being that this decline had recently taken plac.s, and that the firm whose name was mentioned appeared to be giving immediate effect to it in the shape of reduced prices of soap to their customers. As a matter of fact the decline in the prices of raw materials commenced, as stated, nearly 18 months ago, but there had recently been a considerable recovery from the lowest prices touched. More than a year ago Crostields, along with other leading soap manufacturers, having in view the falling prices of raw materials, reduced" Perfection" soap from 3d. to .3id. per lb tablet, and other soaps in like proportion, _
A Refreshing Drink and a Sustaining Food.

div.head: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
div.p: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
XII.-1 f Customs duties make work, why should not Scotland "make work" for the Scots by taxing Imports of English goods P

Protectionists have not sufficient faith in their own "principles." England is a much fiercer competitor of Scotland than is Germany or France. If, then, it would "make work" in Scotland to keep out a few French or German goods, how much more work it would make in Scotland to keep out the many English goods that pass every day over the Scots border. Ireland, also, it is clear, ought to have import duties against both England and Scotland if " Tariff Reform" is true, for most of the goods imported into Ireland come from England. L. G. C. IL

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. Tariff Reformers and Trade Returns.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. Tariff Reformers and Trade Returns.

Sir,—Mr G. H. W. Steel in replying to ray letter, though failing to answer it, yet raised some interesting points. He states in the latter part of his letter that " We Tariff Reformers say that the fundamental argument for Protection is its benefits to labour." This is great news. Will he kindly adduce some evidence in support of it? I have failed in all my examination of economics to find any, and in fact all the evidence is the other way. How is it,l ask him if his contention is correct, that for years past and also to-day, there is a greater number of unemployed in Protected United States than there are in Free Trade England. And in fact all countries are troubled to-day with this problem. It is evident that the solution ot it is by the road of Tariff Reform which is a kind of " Will of the Wisp "being a false light which if adopted will increase the burdens of the people and create greater poverty in our midst.—Yours faithfully, E. ENGLAND.

Rev. J, F. Matthews. Proposed Testimonial. Dear Sir,—Would you kindly permit us to use your paper as a medium to put before the people of Warring- ton the following matters. It is generally known that the Rev. J. Francis Matthews is about to leave the town in consequence of his appointment to an important Baptist Church in Sheffield. It has been suggested to some of us that many friends of Mr. Matthews outside his own church would like to take advantage of this opportunity by contributing to a testimonial, to be given to him as a tangible expression of the high esteem in which he is held by very many in the borough. During the eleven sears that Mr. Matthews has been in Warrington he has been much more than a minister of a Baptist Church; he has made every Church his debtor, and every good cause has received his willing help. He has taken an active interest in civic and social matters and has ever been ready to lend a help- ing hand to anything that would tend to uplift and be to the welfare and happiness of his fellow townsmen. Even those with whom he has differed most have learnt to esteem him as one who is loyal to the -truth as he perceives it, and courteous in the setting of it forth. We feel sure that there will be a ready response to the proposed effort and Mr. William Roberts, Bridge-street, has kindly consented to receive any amount, email and large, towards the proposed gift. We understand that Mr. Matthews leaves the town at the end of this month UHARLES E. DARKER, ARTHUR MOUNFIELD, JAMES BALL, WILLIAM ROBERTS. January 7th, 1909.

div.head: Incipient Romanism at the Parish Church.
div.p: Incipient Romanism at the Parish Church.

• ---- Sir,—l am obliged to you for the insertion of •my letter in your last issue, calling attention to the incipient Rorcanism practised at the Parish Church. ' I write now to enter my protest against the unfair action of your stately contemporary the .‘ Guardian." A copy of my letter, together with that of Rev. John Yonge, was, I understand, sent to the "Guardian ' office, by your messenger, but only that of Mr. Yonge was permitted a place in its privileged columns. Now, sir, if this were the only or first occasion when communications from nay pen were so treated, some reasonable excuse could be sug- gested, but during tbe past five years several letters, containing matters I have considered to be of public interest, have met with the same summary treatment. Why? As a Protestant Churchman it is not difficult to -find a reason. Evangelical or Protestant Churchman- hip need expect but little support from that quarter. The fact that the Church's grip of the congregations Is maintained by ornate and unscriptural forms of service, augmented by the unholy card-party, whist drive and dance is pitiable enough, and we get weekly reports of these things act nauseam. These are practices which Dr. Nixon, Bishop of Jarrow,condemns as the very antithesis of Christianity. Surely these privileged persons are not immune from criticism because of their cloistered virtue. It is true very few Warringtonians are interested in the artistic trivialities to which I referred, but there are some things which do not redound to the credit of this enlightened age I "While men slept, the enemy sowed tares," etc., etc.—Yours, etc., FRANK VAUGHAN. January 7th, 1908.

div.head: LATE MR. GEORGE THOMPSON.
div.p: THE LATE MR. GEORGE THOMPSON.
A Former Warrington Guardian.

The remains were laid to rest in the Chester Cemetery on Saturday of the late Mr. George Thompson, formerly of Derby House, Great Sankey, who passed away at his residence, 19, Cheney-road, Chester, the previous Wednesday morning at the age of sixty-six years. The deceased gentleman, who was a native of Chester, came to Warrington about eighteen years ago to take up the position of outside manager at the Mersey White Lead Works. His conscientious devotion to duty and kindly treatment of the employees earned for him general respect and during his manage- ment the concern made great headway until it now holds a very prominent position amongst the industries of the district. Mr. Thompson acted as secretary of the works sick and burial club and his services were fittingly recognized in December, 1897, by the presentation to him of a handsome silver tea and coffee service. Mr. Thompson always had the interests of the Warrington Infirmary closely at heart, and as a member of the Board of Management and of the Workingmen's Committee he lost no oppor- tnnity of pleading the claims of the institution. He played a most useful part in public life, having served the district of Great Sankey on the Parish Council, Warrington Board of Guardians, and Rural District Council. He was also a member of the Committee of Management of the Warrington Savings Bank. A staunch Wesleyan Methodist, he had a great affection for Bold-street Church, which he regularly attended. The broadness of his sympathies wag, however, shown by the fact that he took a keen and active interest in the formation of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. In -politics he was a Liberal. Failing health compelled film to retire from his position at the Lead Works about eighteen months ago,when he returned to Chester. There be lived in retirement, the only public work in which be took part being that of the committee of the Christian Temperance Society. He leaves a widow and one daughter. Prior to the interment a service was held in the St. John-street Wesleyan Chapel, the officiating ministers being the Rev. E. Wright Fladcock, and Rev. S. G. _Haywood (Wesleyan Ministers), and Rev. J. J Hargreaves (Grosvenor Park Baptist Church.) The chief mourners were: Mr. W. G. Thompson (Sheffield), Mr. Joseph Thompson (Manchester), Mr. Joseph Davies, Mr. John Evans, Mr. J. Ward Jones, Mr. Thomas Melbourne. The deceased's brother, the Rev. W. H. Thcmpson, who belongs to the Wesleyan ministry, was unavoidably absent. Other friends present included :—Rev. J. J. Hargreaves (chairman of the Chester Band of Hope Union), Messrs. J. Bennion (secretary of the Union),T. Kendall, J. Shires J. Priddley, Beresford, Adams, R. Wallace and E. Walker (representing the Chester Christian Temper- ance Society), Robert Davies, F. Lloyd, George Gough, T. Bradburn, H. Gandy (representing the Chester Medical Association), T. Sconce and Enos Jones (representing the" Earl of Chester" Lodge of the G.U.0.0.F.), W. Shingler, S. Harding, William, James and John Melbourne (of the firm of Messrs. J. Melbourne, Limited, Warrington), Sloane (representing the Mersey White Lead Works, Great Sankey), T. Ashley, W. Jackson, M. Geurdon, W. Skelhorn, H. Taylor, A. Oldfield. Wreaths were sent by the widow and daughter, Miss Lloyd, Mr. Gorse (Warrington), Mr. Sloane, and Mr. Frith (per Mersey White Lead Works), Mr. and Mrs. Jackson (warrington) Mr. T. Bradburn and family, Rev. W. H. and Mrs. Thompson Mr. and Mrs. Evans, Miss Johnson tQueen's-aven no

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST MR. LOUIS
div.p: THE CHARGE AGAINST MR. LOUIS
HENSHALL
Further Remand.

The Warrington Police Court was again crowded yesterday when Mr. Louis Henshall, director and manager of Messrs. R. A. Naylor, Limited, timber merchants, Howley, surrendered to his bail on the charge of stealing £79 95., the moneys of the firm. Mr. Padmore (Messrs. Tatham, Worthington and Co., Manchester) sppeared for the prosecution and Mr. r S. Steel represented the defendant. The magistrates on the bench were :—the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) Aldermen Smethurst and Burton, Councillor Evans Messrs. H. Thornton, G. Pilling, C. Jackson Holmes, A. J. Jolley and W. Furness. Mr. Steel said be was sorry to say it would b impossible to go on with the case that day. He had briefed learned council to appear for Mr. Henshall but unfortunately it was not convenient for him to attend. Further than that, some further charges that were to be made against Mr. Henshall were only delivered to him (Mr. Steel) on Wednesday and they had not yet had the opportunity of going fully into them and pre- paring the defence. His application was that the Bench would allow the case to stand adjourned until Tuesday next when they hoped a part of the case would be proceeded with. He understood there was no objection on the part of the prosecution. Mr. Padmore said he had no objection to the adjournment but he should have delivered his charges earlier if Mr. Steel had not asked for the case to stand over. He did not want it putting on his shoulders that he was keeping the case back. He consented to an adjournment until Tuesday but then he must go on with it. _ _ _

......... Mr. Steel : I don't want to suggest it is the fault of Mr. Padmore. I was only telling you the circum- stances as they stand at the moment. Mr, lienshall was then remanded until Tuesday on the same bail as before —himself in Zl,OOO and two other sureties of IV edch.

div.head: WORKS ASSESSMENTS.
div.p: WORKS ASSESSMENTS.
Important Appeals at Warrington. MANUFACTURERS AND HIGH RATES.

A meetin2 of the Warrington Union Assessment Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterdiy, Mr. J. Billinge presiding. There were also present : Messrs. A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, A. Brooks, W. Furness, W. Gill, J. Evans, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. R. Meacock (valuer), W. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer for War- rington) and F. Wright (assistant overseer for Poulton- with-Fearnhead).

FIRTH CO , LTD. Mr. T. P. RATIIBONE appealed on behalf of the Firth Co., Ltd., wire manufacturers, Howley, against the assessment of gross £1092, rateable £B2l. He said the increase in the assessment represented 262 per cont. When the company occupied a mill on Friars Green they paid a rent of £l4O and were assessed at gross £169 10s., , net £139. The premises they were now occupying were about three times the size of the Friars Green mill, and since that time-1895—their output had increased from 91 to 3 times. If they took their assessment on the same basis it would bring it up. no £382 n-+ out the Committee's proposal was + increase it to £B2l. The buildings yet fully occupied, and a considerable 4. 4, porvion • tne plant was standing. As a cotton mill the buildings were only assessed at gross £429, net £328. The present was a very inopportune time for an increase, and he contended that the increase was out of all proportion to their business. The wire busi- ness hod not been a very profitable one in Warrington. rhe' Committee deckled to adjourn the case for a month so that the valuer could confer with the firm. PEARSON AND KNOWLES COAL AND IRON CO., LTD. Mr. JAMES DODDS appealed on behalf of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co, Ltd., against the assessment of the works in Bewsey-road and Dallam- lane, (late Smith) •;fhich figured in the list at £11,178 gross and £7,439 rateable. The VALUER advised that in view of certain circum- stances the assessment should be reduced to gross £10,902, rateable £6,707. Mr. DODDS said they had met Mr. Meacock and they understood he was prepared to make some concession on the assessment as it stood in the list. The very large increase brought out in the new valuation was a great surprise to them, in face of the fact that their works were not now producing, nor were they capable of producing more iron and steel than they were 20 years ago. This they proved to Mr. Meacock by the actual returns for each of the last 20 years. No doubt they had been building over that period, but there had been corresponding removals; so that the increased valuation must largely be the result of a wider interpretation of the meaning of such words as heredita- ments, and, from the firm's point of view, the straining of such bases as might exist for these assessments. They demurred to man); of the details of IVlr.Meacock's valuation, as being considerably too high, and as being, from their experience and reading of the law and practice of rating, improperly taken to account. Nevertheless, they were prepared, pro- visionally and under protest, to accept his figures for the purpose of the new assessment, while reserving to themselves the right to re-open the question should they be so advised in the event of the valuations of other works turning out to be inadequate and not in proportion to their own. Having said that, they desire to testify to the care and ability brought to the valua- tion of their premises by Mr. Meacock. He spent very many days during several months in their works, and from the discussions they had subsequently had with him, and from his complete details of the various figures, astd the plans he had prepared, he (Mr. Dodds) was satisfied that, so far as the firm was concerned, and apart from differences of view, Mr. Meacock had done his work conscientiously and thoroughly. The committee agreed to the amended valuation of £10,902 gross and £6,707 rateable. RYLANDS BROS., LTD. Mr. W. PBTER RYLANDS appealed On behalf of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd., against the assessment , of the works in Church-street and Dalton Bank which ' stood at £9,764 gross £7,250 rateable. He said he had bad several agreeable interviews with Mr. Meacock who had met him in a most reasonable spirit and he believed Mr. Meacock would be prepared to make modifications owing to the information he (Mr. Rylands) bad given him as to the cost of maintenance of certain branches of the business. The amended valuntion,however, would still leave a wide discrepancy between chat he (Mr. Rylands) thought would be a fair and just figure and the one Mr. Meacock had arrived at. As a leading manufacturer of Warrington he wished to address a few general considerations to the comtr ittee. The effect of a high scale of assess- ment was two-fold. In the first place, it was important, to the town that it should have as many prosper- ous industries as possible, as the private individual and the shopkeeper depended for their very existence upon the presence of these -manufactures. Consequently it was to the interest of the ruling authorities of the town that as many industries and as many of as successful a character as possible should exist within the town's borders. If a firm of capitalists were anxious to start a new works they looked round for a suitable place and one of the first things they asked was "What is the scale of assessment, and what are the rates actually charged ? " A high scale of assessment had an extremely deterrent effect upon enterprising men who were anxious to find a place in which to erect their works. Moreover the effect of high assessments went beyond the mere checking of the creation of new enterprises. From time to time businesses came to grief owing to stress of competition and difficulties of trade and every additional burden that was put upon the shoulders of the businesses as a whole would increase the number of those who came to grief and bring them to grief at an earlier date than otherwise. It was a point that deserved consideration as to the effect of putting heavy burdens upon manufacturers lest the cow which was giving the milk should be killed. The burden of rates was an element in the cost of manufacture and had to be taken into consideration by the man who was selling his commodities just as much as any other cost of any of his processes, and if the rates were very high the manufacturer was placed in an inferior position to compete with foreigners and with manufacturers in other towns.' Orders were lost which otherwise the manufacturer would have secured and the consequence was that the wages which would have been paid in the execution of such orders were lost to the tradespeople and shop-owners in Warrington. Mr. Rylands appealed against the assessment of his firm's works on the ground that the figures on which the valua- tion was based were excessive and there were special circumstances connected with the works. One special circumstance which Mr. Rylands mentioned was that Messrs. Rylands Bros.,who could claim to be the leading wire netting manufacturers in the world, had hitherto been largely dependent upon the supply of German wire to keep that branch of their trade going. They had bought it oftener than not at a cheaper price delivered at their own works than they could produce it them- selves. There was always the possibility of the Germans raising the price by forming a syndicate, and in that event they as netting manufacturers dependent upon them for raw material would be almost certain to be extinguished. To safeguard their position Messrs. Rylands Bros. had erected a new department with the necessary plant at a cost of £50,000 to produce the wire themselves. The new works were therefore net put down to produce a commodity for sale, but for their own consumption. He submitted that a figure not higher than £4,220 but very much nearer the rateable value of £3,470 10s. as it was up to recently, would be a fair assessment. The committee decided to reduce the rateable assessment to £6,000. The CHAIRMAN told Mr. Rylands they were delighted to know that extensions were being made at

the works and they anticipated that the assesssment might grow in the future. Mr. RYLANDs said be was obliged to the committee for their sympathetic hearing, but they could not expect him to see eye to eye with them in the matter. Mr. FURNESS said the committee were obliged to Mr. Rylands for his instructive address.

MONKS, HALL AND CO., LTD. Mr. F. IL MoNKs appealed on behalf of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Limited, against the assesement of their works at £8,517 gross and £6,186 rateable. At his suggestion the case was adjourned for a month in order that he might havei,he opportunity of going more fully into bhe particulars with Mr.Meacock.

OTHER. APPEILS. The cases of the ‘Varrington Wire Rope Co., Ltd., Bewsey-road (2141 gross and £361 rateable), and the Longford Wire Co., Ltd, Longford, (£2141 gross and £1.664 rateable) were also adjourned for a month.
The Examiner, Saturday, January 9, 1909.

Brooks, J. Backhouse, G. Mather, J. Ball, W. Houghton, W. Stanier, J. C. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer of health), 13. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances).

div.head: SANKF.Y CANAL BRIDGE.
div.p: SANKF.Y CANAL BRIDGE.

The CLERIC said nothing further had transpired with regard to this question except that Mr. Harcourt E. Clare, Clerk to the Lancashire County Council, applied to him by telephone a few days ago for a copy of the old Sankey Canal Act. He (Mr. Sutton) informed him he had not got a copy. It was evident that the County Council, were taking steps in the matter. Mr. FORSII4IV : I keep iute.rviewing them and trying to get along with it. The SURVEYOR said he had supplied Mr. Compton Hall, the County Bridgeniaster, with extracts from the old Act.

THE NEW BYE-LAWS. The CLERK reported that he had received a letter from the Local Government Board regarding the new bye-laws with respect to new streets, buildings, 84c., and making eertain alterations. Mr. BrtooKs said the bye-laws now met the wishes of the Council and he had pleasure in moving that preliminary steps be taken to put them into force and that a copy of the bye-laws be forwarded to each mem- ber of the Council at the earliest, possible date. Mr. FURNESS seconded. The CLERK stated that it would be necessary to publish the bye-laws and to obtain certain Urban powers before they could enforce them.

The resolution was agreed to. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Brooks, the Clerk and the Surveyor had done a great deal of work in connection with the drawing up of the bye-laws and he moved that the best thanks of the Council be accorded to them for the excessive trouble they had gone to in the matter. Mr. MATHER seconded and said the Council ought to feel proud of and thankful to these gentlemen. They owed them a deep debt of gratitude, and especially Mr. Brooks. The time had now gone by for jerry-builders to work aswthey had done in the district. Mr. BALL and Mr. FURNESS briefly supported. _ Mr. FORSHA.W, also supporting? said Mr. 117:Jo.lis had a highly developed knowledge Oh these matters and was invaluable to the Council, He was certainly serving his day and generation to the best of his ability. The 1,5u3 was heart;24 accorded. THI3 OT OF ROAD MAINTENANCE. _ _ _ COUNTY COUNCIL CRITICISED.

Mr. 13itooKs moved : "That; this Council requests the County Council to put the portion of the Liverpool and Manchester-road situated in the parish of Rixton in a reasonable state of repair." He said he had brought the resolution as a last resource. He had used all the methods by which they usually got their grievances redressed. He had badgered Mr. Newcombe for the past two and a half years, and Mr. Newcombe had carried a great deal of that badgering to the higher authority. He (Mr. Brooks) had been a nuisance to the County Councillor for the district (Mr. Forshaw) ever since he achieved the distinction, and Mr. Forshaw had done what he could in the matter. Although the matter appeared to pertain to one parish only it appeared to him that their po3itlon as a road authority and their relationships with the County Council were to some extent bound up with the resolution. He need not tell them of the great increase in the wear and tear of the roads. It was common knowledge that there was no comparison whatever between the position at present and what it was even four or five years ago. He asked them to support the resolution because' under the conditions which were coming into existense the road in Rixton to-day was only what the roads throughout the district would be in the near future, judging from what appeared to be the policy of the County Council. The Warrington Rural district was situated between two of the greatest centres of population in the country. There was quite a procession of heavy traffic through the district ; that procession was increased by the local traffic of Warrington and Wicines gnd three-fourths of their main roads were being mangled in a manner which three or four years ago did not seem possible. This question would be serious enough in all conscience if the Road Locomotives Act were put into operation but it appeared to be the policy of the County Council to allow any weight to use the roads. During the last year one load which was nearly three times the maximum allowed Tinder the Road Loco- motives Act passed thorough the district from Sankey to Rixton. Their officials were alert and the Surveyor went and made a personal inspection to see the excess of the load. He also got into communication with the County Hundred Surveyor and had him as an eye witness. The matter was reported to the County Council but no action was taken. The inference was apparent. Under those circumstances one would expect that the allowance by the County to various local authorities would have increased very much during the past few years and that ins district like the Warrington Rural district with three fourths of their roads under the new usage it would not be a matter of increasing by leaps and bounds but of the grants nearly doubling themselves. Strange to say, their nominal allowance had not increased by one penny. True, they had had special grants but they had not been sufficient and the were quite a misnomer. When the District Council flr y took over the roads the special grants were for species purposes, for strengthening, improving, widening and i matters of that kind, but to-day they were given to eke out an absurdly insufficient allowance. The only " special "property he saw about them was that they were specially insufficient to do even that. If the "specials," added to their allowance, were sufficient he would not quarrel with the name, but it was demoralizing to give an insufficiency of money for a purpose, practically to assume that the money was sufficient, and then eke it out with the special grants. It was demoralizing from a financial point of view and from the practical working standpoint. They should set their faces against it and work in future for something like a sufficient grant for roads in repair. Whether they were likely to get that was eloquently told by a few statistics contained in the County Treasurer's reports. In 1903 there was spent on county main roads in ordinary expenditure £147,000 odd and in extra expenditure £30,000, total £177,000 ; in 1901, ordinary expenditure £157,000, extra expenditure £17,500, total £174,000. In 1908 the expenditure had dropped to £151,000 but payments were made to the extent of £157,000. In the Warrington Rural District the expenditure in 1904 was £2,000 and in 1908 £2,350, so that they were well off in comparison with the remainder of the County. They might in the near future have to reconsider their relations with the County Council. He for one did not feel inclined to be a member of any Council which had to incur the odium of badly done work and undoubtedly that Council must either do its work badly or have a much larger grant. He would not like_to accompany the resolution with a threat but they ought to feel that on the issue of that request would to a great extent depend their future relations with the County. Mr. HOUGHTON seconded.

FortsilAw : Is the portion of the road referred to in a worse state than other portions between Rixtoa and Warrington? Mr. IlnooKs : Undoubtedly. The SURVEYOR : It is undoubtedly the worst part, but it is all getting like that. Mr. BRooK's said they had been told that good roads were to radiate from Warrington. To Rixton might be applied the line : " Man never is but always to be blessed." The roads were getting like porridge in wet weather,and dust in dry weather. Mf. FortsllAw : Other places are as far in the soup as Rixton.

Mr. BROOKES : No, but they are gradually getting so. The CHAIRMAN : There is no doubt they are all going the same way. Mr. FORSIIAW : The same condition of things obtains practically all over the county. Mr. BROOKS : If the County Council is going to let the matter get into this position let the County Council be responsible for it and bear the odium. Mr. HOUGHTON suggested that the County Council ought to revise its bye-laws and stop the heavy traffic. Mr. BROOKS: They have no need to revise their bye-laws. The Act is sufficient but they don't put it into force.

Mr. lioucToN said the neighbouring Rural District Council of Runcorn recovered regularly from people who damaged the roads and he did not know why the Warrington District Council should not do the same. Mr. BROOKS: We cannot recover anything on the main roads, it must be recovered by the County Council. They are ignoring the Locomotives Act. The resolution was carried unanimously with the following addition : "That Messrs. Brooks and Furness be deputed to attend with the Surveyor before the County Main Roads Committee to urge the adoption of early measures in that behalf, and that the attendance of the County Councillor (Mr. Forshaw) be re quested.

div.head: OLD FOLK'S TREAT.
div.p: OLD FOLK'S TREAT.
HAPPY GATHERINGS AT THE PARR HALL.

About 1,300 of Warrington's old folk were enter- tained right royally at the Parr Hall on Thursday, and the scene at either of the gatherings —the old men's dinner and the aged women's tea —was enough to do one's heart good. It showed that the spirit of true benevolence is not yet dead. The sole idea which animated the affair was to make the day a happy one for toil-worn veterans and ancient dames, and to this end a large body of workers put forth their best efforts with conspicuous success. It speaks well for the generosity of the townspeople that for so many years funds have always been forthcoming to provide this New Year treat, and to say that it is highly appreciated by the old folk is to put the case very mildly. Their faces beamed with pleasure and gratitnde, and one felt it would indeed be a pity to deny them this little festivity which is so eagerly looked forward to. At noon 650 old men sat down to a good old English dinner of roast beef, pork, mutton, vegetables , and plum pudding, with an allowance of beer. It was a motley assembly. Grey and wrinkled, many of the men were bent with infirmity whilst others still carried themselves erect. Some were army veterans ' who proudly displayed medals —the reminders of many a great campaign. The oldest guest was 91 years of age and there was quite a good number over eighty. A prominent figure was Mr. John Drury, the well known temperance worker, who is 85 years of age and has been a teetotaller for 51 years. A busy band of helpers waited upon the guests,amongst those , present being the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs, F9rfshaw), Alderman Smethurst (president of th,7l committee) anti Mrs. Smethurst and most of the members of the committed uhich, addition to the names already gives, is as follows Vice-president, Mr. Richard Shackleton ; hon.treasurer Councillor Nield ; hon. secretary, Mr. T. A. Sutton ; Alderman Burton, Councillor Rogers, Captain Potter, Messrs. C. E. Bunch, Harry Hope, Thomas Atherton, Alfred Jolley, Thomas Bowers, Thomas Locker, William Webster and Samual Davies. While the meal was in progress, a capital programme of organ music was played by Mr. J. A. Jones, Dinner over, there was a little speech-making. Alderman SMEITLIIIRST (the President) once more ' wished all present a happy and prosperous New Year. They were extremely obliged to all the ladies and gentlemen, and particularly the Mayor and Mayoress, who had helped to serve the dinner out. Unfortun- ately many of the old men who were present last year were not with them that day. They had gone on their long journey. Might God spare most of those who formed the gathering that day, to assemble next year. There were over GOO present at the dinner. He was sorry in one sense that the number was so large but it was gratifying that owing to the deep interest taken in the committee by the townspeople they were able to give such a treat. The subscribers had again given most liberally. (Applause.) There were many old men present who would now be able to live more comfort- ably from one week's end to another, owing to the old age pensions, There were a large number in that aSSAmi.y?.- who ila i the übs seventy. It i s wonderful i how thesethingsdwornkrtidd "h worked on a few who had said the committee would not need subscriptions now because the men had pensions. In reply to that he would say that there were a great many under seventy years of age and those who thought their subscriptions would not be required wore making a great mistake. They would be as urgently needed as ever they were before. (Applause) He had sent letters far and wide to old friends of that institution and had received some beautiful responses and handsome cheques. The present committee was the third which had been formed since his association with the treat and he was happy to say they had not lost a single member during the past year. The president con- cluded by proposing the health of "The King and Queen and members of the Royal family," which was enthusiastically honoured. The MAYOR, who had a hearty reception addressed the guests as "gentlemen," remarking that they were well entitled to be called gentlemen because he knew they had lived a long and clean life. He joined with the President in wishing them a very happy New Year. There could be no doubt that the treat was a very excellent institution and he wished it came oftener than once a year. (Applause) He had pleasure in propos- ing a vote of thanks to their worthy President who had devoted so much time to getting in subscriptions (Applause). Mr. I. JOHNSON, one of the guests, seconded and said Alderman Smethurst gained the affections of the people of Warrington during his two years as Mayor. He had the old people's welfare very much at heart and as an illustration he (Mr. Johnson) might mention that when he went to the General Post Office last Friday—they knew what for—(laughter and applause)—he was delighted to see Alderman Smethnrst signing pension books for men and women who were unable to write, and the task seemed to afford him the greatest pleasure. They hoped he Would be spared fora long tiine and that at last his sun would set in a clear sky and he would " pass through death triumphant home." (Applause.) The MAYOR said Alderman Smethurst was seventy years of age and looked remarkably well. (Applause.) The vote was carried with great enthusiasm. Mr. H. Boa read letters from two military veterans —Mr. Harold W. Hardy and Mr. Robert Scotter— thanking the President for his invitation to attend and regretting that owing to infirmity they could not accept. The old men having filed out of the hall dinner was provided for a large number of unemployed who had gathered outside the hall. In the evening about 650 aged women sat down to a substantial tea, consisting of sandwiches, currant and seed cake. The oldest guest was 92 years of age. An entertainment to which the public were admitted,

followed. Alderman S METHURST, having wished all present a happy New Year, proposed a hearty vote of thanks to I the subscribers and helpers, and this was heartily carried. Continuing. the President said he had been connected with the treat for twenty-eight years, and he had never before seen such a large attendance as they had had that day owing to the distress. Altogether about 1,300 old men and women had been entertained, and the Committee had relaxed their rules in one res- pect, inasmuch as they had provided some poor people under i sixty years of age with dinner and tea. He believed this was the oldest continuous institution of the kind in Lancashire, and they bad never yet appealed. in vain for funds. The President paid a high compli- ment to the Mayor and Arayoress, and thanked them for their presence. The entertainment proved one of the most successful on record and afforded great delight to the old ladies and to the public. The committee were very fortunate in securing the services of artistes from the Palace and Hippodrome and Royal Court Theatre, by kind per- mission of Mr. F. Macnaghten and Mr. Wentworth Croke. Mollie and Winnie Brooke, dainty vocalists and dancers opened the programme with a bright turn; and the Garricks, in their charming song scene, had a great reception. Russell Brandow, colcured dancing comedian, aroused great enthusiasm by his wonder- fully clever performance, and J. H. Greener, the premier singing pit lad (who has actually worked in the mine and has raised a large sum on behalf of the sufferers by the Maypole disaster) pleased all with his homely songs. Lockhart's " Baby " elephant, introduced by Captain Taylor, came across from the Palace and partook of a hearty supper in view of the audience. None of the old ladies, -however, accepted Alderman Sraethnrst's genial prop:sal that they should have a ride on "Baby's" hack. Miss M. Julia Willis, a talented member of" The Bondman" company, with a sweet and powerful voice,sang a couple of songs and Miss Gertrude Helene and Master Walter Neville, two youthful per- forrners in the same company, fairly captivated the audience with their quaint songs, while the little girl excelled herself in a pretty dance. A number of young ladies and gentlemen who are students of the Warrington School of Music (the principals of which are the Misses Sutton) gave that sprightly number from" Florodora"—" Tell me pretty maiden " —in vivacious and altogether pleasing style,and received a hearty encore. Later the young ladies acquitted themselves splendidly in a coon song and dance, the soloist being Miss Davenport, and this item also had to be repeated. Aliso Davenport's interpretation of Tosti's " Good-bye" was most effective, The humor- ous items by Mr. J. Emson and Mr. W. W. Whittle con- vulsed the audience with merriment and throughout the whole entertainment there was not a dull moment. Mr. Norman Latham was an efficient accompanist. Before the proceedings closed The MAYOR re-echoed Alderman Smethurst's good wishes to the guests and at his suggestion a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Alderman Smethurst, the artistes, Councillor Rogers and all who had assisted in arranging the entertainment. Before leaving each old lady was presented with an orange.

div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHURCPI.—The choir of this church went out carol singing at Christma.s time with the object of raising funds for the purchase of a piano. The effort was much appreciated and a sum of nearly £l6 was raised. UNITED WATCHNIGHT SERVICE.—A united watchnight service in which the members of the two Methodist Churches and a number of members of the Anglican Church took part was held at the Independent Metho- dist Church on New Year's Eve. Mr. A. Mounfield conducted the meeting and gave an address from the text " Behold I have set before thee an upen door." Mr. R. B. Woods also gave a brief address. After the stroke of midnight the large assembly sang" Come, let us anew," with great feeling.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Bondman."

Both as novelist and dramatist Mr. Hall Caine always grips the heart of the multitude and his stage version of "The Bondman" which is presented at the Royal Court Theatre this week by Mr. Wentworth Croke's company, rivals most modern dramas in popu- larity. It is the story of a great act of self-effacement, showing how a bitter feud between two half-brothers gives place to love and prompts one to sacrifice all that men count most dear for the sake of the other against whom be had previously harboured murderous designs. Though the end comes somewhat abruptly and leaves a sense of disappointment, still it is a powerful if not a great play, and large audiences have acclaimed it with enthusiasm this week. Dominating the whole action of the story is the solitary and pathetic figure of Jason— the man who is robbed of his birthright and who, when long-denied happiness at last seems within his grasp,_ is deprived of that too. We could hardly imagine a finer study of the character than Mr. R. Scrope Quentin's. By voice and bearing

div.p: MISS ENRIQUETI-k. CRICEITON, PRIMA DONNA,
GRAND OPERA. WEEK AT WARRINGTON. A FESTIVAL OF MUSIC.

One of the chief local bookings of recent years that announced for next week at the Court P r..taea.re, when the world famed Moody-Manners crand Opera Company will pay its first visit to Tvarrington. No fewer than seven grand operas which were selected by he majority of voters, vri..l be rendered. The operas are the same as thoa, performed at the Covent Garden, Drury-lane ar..ti Lyric Theatres, London, but the represGnrations of the Moody-Manners Opera Company, have the advantage for the ordinary English playgoer who is not a good linguist —they are given in English. The principals are all first-class artistes the chorus is one of the best in England, and the staging and dresses will be on a scale never attempted before at Warrington. This organization numbers 70 members, including a double set of principals,a chorus of 40, a full corps de ballet, and 15 musicians to augment the local theatre orchestra, thus making in all an assembly of 25 rausicans. It is a well-known fact that the performances of the Moody-Manners Opera Companies are noticeable for their excellent ensembles. With them the opera is the motif and not the individual, their representation being a liberal education to the multitude. Even the most critical would be well advised to pay a visit to one of these operas to be rendered by this famous
AS MADAME BUTTERFLY.

erganieatin, and we can confidently say,• that when the cu'..."(ain drops for the finale on Saturday evening 17..,5t, their hunger for Grand Opera in English with British artistes will not diminish. The Moody- Manners companies are the largest English Opera Companies that have ever travelled throughout Great Brithin and the Colonies. We sincerely trust that they will be well patronised by the inhabitants in and around Warrington, so that it may be known that Warrington can claim to have an annual week of grand operas in English as well as other towns close by. In this approahing visit we are promised th e production here for the first time in English of Puccini's thrilling opera " Madame Butterfly which finds such a keen admirer as Queen Alexander on its production at the Covent Garden Opera House, London.

The following works have been selected by the majority of voters, and will be rendered in the fol- lowing order : —Monday,Bizet's "Carmen " ; Tuesday, Wagner's, " Lobengria " ; Wednesday, Pucciai's "Madame Butterfly "for the first time in English ; Thursday, Gounod's " Faust " ; Friday, Wagner's " Taunhanser " ; Saturday Matinee, " Maiame Butterfly" will be repeated ; Evening, Balfe's "Bohemian Girl " will end a grand musical week rarely to be had in Warrington. Mr. Cuthber t Hanley is the Musical Director, The Box Office is now open.

Miss Georgina Winter is a charming ' erreeba and interprets the varying moods of the part to advantage. She can be vivaciovs as well as tragic and does not oppress one with sustained lugubrious- ness. Mr. W. H. Rotherham makes a brilliant success of the dual role of Grandfather and Father Ferrati. His portrayal of the ancient tar smacks of the sea while as the fallen priest whose self-respect is restored through a single act of trust and kindness he is equally clever. Miss Madge Lanerton as the loquacious and match-making Mrs. Fairbrother creates many a ripple of merriment, and her solemn-visaged husband Adam Fairbrother, who is ever quoting Scripture, is well impersonated by Mr. Oswald Lino.ard. Mr. W. Henry HarF,reaves makes the most of the part of Michael Sunlocks and quickly enlists the favour of the audience. The play is splendidly mounted and nothing more elaborate in the way of scenic effects has been seen in Warrington. The representation of the Sulphur Mines, with the awsome explosion, is a triumph in stage craft. In every respect the production is thoroughly adequate and those who have not already seen it should take the opportunity of doing so this (Saturday) evening.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
CONSERVATIVE MINISTRY FORMED.

The Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society -will resume its deliberations in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club on Thursday evening and an interesting session is in prospect. The Conservative party will take office and their programme will be outlined in the King's Speech to be submitted on Thursday. We understand that the Ministry has been formed as follows:

div.head: FRENZIED MAN AND THE SOLICITOR.
div.p: FRENZIED MAN AND THE SOLICITOR.
Violent, Scene in a :Warrington Office.

A violent scene occurred shortly before noon oat Wednesday at the office of Councillor Thomas S. Steel, solicitor, Mill street, Warrington. It appears that Mr. G. H. Warburton Steel, Councillor Steel's younger brother who works with him, was in hio room when he received an unannounced call from Ur. Alfred Dakin a powerfully built farmer, of Orford, who demanded the sum of £7O, which he said he had left there. He added that unless he got that sum he would cut his (Mr. Steel's) heart out and cut his throat. Mr. Steel, thinking the man was mad, told him he should have the money if he stepped into the general office. Accordingly he conducted Dakin into the general office, where a number of clients were waiting. Councillor Steel had occasion to go into this office from his own private room,when Dakin,who was wearing a big cape and carrying a heavy stick, rushed at him, making some incoherent remarks about £7O. Mr Steel told him he had better go and consult his own solicitor, Mr. Fox. Dakin then said he was going. to have the £7O, and endeavoured to force his way into the private office, adding that if he did not get the money he would stab Mr. Steel. He began to fumble under his cape, and then Mr. Steel struggled with him, eventually gaining access to his office and keeping the man outside. Councillor Pemberton was waiting to see Mr. Steel, - and he asked Dakin to be quiet. Dakin said, "Do you say that ?" and Mr. Pemberton replied "Yes." Dakin then whipped out a knife from under his coat and made a lunge with it at Mr. Pemberton, who alertly stepped back, but the weapon :grazed his coat, and he rushed down two flights of stairs into the street.Dakin followed, but stumbled on the second flight. On. getting up he ran into the street, and the outer door of the office was promptly closed. Dakin remained at the door with the knife in his hand, declaring that if he could get in he would murder Mr. Steel, and that if he could not get at him to stab him he would get a revolver to shoot him. The police were telephoned for and Sergeant Heap, the biggest man i the borough force, and several county constables. came upon the scene and seized the man. After a tough struggle he was taken to the Police Station. When searched, three knives, freshly sharpened, were found in his possession, one of which was a cobbler's knife sharpened to a fine point. There is no doubt that if D.Akin had not stumbled on the stairs litr. Pemberton wonld have received' serious injuries. Later in the day Dakin was conveyed to the Work— house where he is still detained. We understand that Mr. Steel has not had any dealings with Dakin, with the exception that eighteen months ago Dakin purchased some property from a client of Mr. Steel, and in the usual course of things he attended at the office to sign the contract and paid a deposit of £7O. Mr. Fox acted for Dakin, and the property was conveyed in the usual way. Mr. Steel has received many letters and telegrams congratulating him on his narrow escape. So early as nine o'clock on Thursday morning a wire came to hand from the Isle of Wight. We hear that owing to Dakin's condition it is not likely that police proceedings will be taken.

div.head: TRAVELLING DRAPER'S FAILURE.
div.p: A TRAVELLING DRAPER'S FAILURE.
Serion Allegation as to Book Debts.

The adjourned public examination of James crozier,- travelling draper, of 49, Museum-street, Warrington, was resumed at the Warrington Bankruptcy Court to-day before Mr. Registrar Ridgway. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for Mr. Daniel Craig, a creditor, and Mr. Ernest Holman Kingdon, another creditor was also present. In reply to the Official Receiver (Mr. J. Grant Gibson) debtor stated that he never told Mr. Kingdon that the furniture in his house belonged to him. The Official Receiver : Did you give Mr. Kingdoa a promissory note for £25, payable in six months? Debtor : I signed one. The note was made by some- one in Manchester, and he did not know the address. lie had not seen the man since, and had no hand in ther manufacture of the note. The note was given to Mr. Kingdon in part discharge of a debt owing by my nephew. The Official Receiver : Mr. Craig has given me the names and addresses of persons to whom clothes are supposed to have been supplied, and in each case the address does not exist. _ _ _

Debtor: The names and addresses were given to me. The Official Receiver : The allegation is that there- are no such numbers in the streets, and that you have created fictitious customers. Debtor: I have never sold any clothes in that way. The Official Receiver : What explanation have you to give of the charge brought by Mr. Craig ? Debtor: Those were the addresses given to me. The Official Receiver: But you must have called upon them. Debtor: Sometimes money was sent down to the house. In reply to further questions he denied that he had ever in his life created fictitious customers. Mr. Browne: I put it to you that the promissory note is an absolute forgery fled swindle between you and your nephew. Debtor : I never got anything out of it. The examination was adjourned, Mr. Browne remark- ing that it was too serious a matter fur it to be closed.

div.head: Penny Popular Concerts.
div.p: Penny Popular Concerts.

There was another large audience at the penny concert in Bold-street school on Saturday evening wheu a popular concert party from St. Helens paid a return visit. The artistes were Madam Edith Hopkinson, Miss Eleanor Slator, and Messrs. Harper, Roberts, Addison, Fritchley, and the Brothers Cross. The Brothers Cross greatly amused the audience with their humorous selections and there was not a dull moment from beginning to end of the programme. LINSEED COMPOITND ' for Coughs and Colds. A PASSING FANCY." Warrington Man's Love Affair. At the Salford liumired Court of Record on Monday, in Mancheiter, Mr. F. Mellor, N.C. (Deputy Judge), and a jury heard an action for breach of promise of marriage. The plaintiff, Agnes Gertrude Bennett, 25 years of age, is (it. was stated) a shop assistant, and the i defendant, Arthur Nield, aged 23 years, was described as an iron moulder formerly a sergeant in the Volunters, of Fletcher-street, Wilderspool, SA'arrington. Gill,ert Jordon represented the plaintiff, and Mr.! Gordon Hewart the defendant. Mr. Jordan said the jury would come to the conclu- sien that the defendant had treated this girl badly. The main factor on which they relied was that he had known her for shout ln years, the parties haying lived near to each other in Salford. For the past eight years they had been "walking out." At Christmas, 1905, he wanted to buy her an engagement tine, but as he was not then twenty-one it was postponed until the May following, when he gave her one on her birthday, with the remark that the next ring that he gave her would be a plain one. In the October of that Tear he obtained her mother's consent to the marriage. 'in July, 1908. he was cool and distant after returning from a cycling tour, and on the 11th July, after they had been to the tlseat re, he refused to go into her home, where he often visited. Pressed by the plaintiff for an explanation, he said, "I am making a change and I shan't see you any more. Try to forget me; you will meet some- one more worthy of you than On being pressed some days later for an explanation of his conduct he "I've taken a fancy to another girl." and then to the plaintiff be added, "This other girl, oh ! I might get tired of her and in two or three months I may tome hack to you."—(Laughter). Mr. Jordan read a letter in which the defendant on July 28th asked if any proceedings were to be taken against him, and added," I hope you are not doing so as it means disgrace for us both." Miss Bennett, how- •ever, took action. In one of his letters he said," I had w hit of luck on the Wednesday as I won the sweep, 10s. —so that's a little bit more to the little lot." Defendant was arcir.king at Warrington, and that had reference to a saving account that was being made between them in view of the wedding-day. The plaintiff said that all the explanation the defendant gave her was that he had"a passing fancy for another girl." (Laughter.) He asked for his ring back lut she did not give in to him. He said that he might come back in about two months. When the writ WRR issued he said he was willing to fulfil his promise. The Deputy Judge: That was two months after.

Mr. Gordon Hewart (in crass-examination) : Are you willing to marry him ?—Not after such 'a trick as that ; I couldn't trust him. Are you well rid of him ?—I don't know, but if hell do that before what will he do afterwards? (Laughter.) You have got rid of an undesirable husband ?—That may I e. Other evidence was given of the promise, and Mr. Gordon Ilewart said it was admitted, and also that ,words than might be construed as a breach of the promise were used by the defendant on July lI.—No evidence was called for the defonce. The jury gave a verdict for plaintiff, and assessed the damages at £35. Military Funeral. With full military honours, the funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday afternoon of the late Colour-Sergeant Jesse Merchant, of Percy- street, who was formerly connected with the South Lancagbire Regiment. The deceased, who was 45 years of age retired on pension in 1902, after having servelef r 20 years, part in the Ist Battalion and part on the permanent staff of the 3rd Battali.n, S .uth Lancashire Regiment. Ho trrved in the latter Battali-n in South Africa during tl'e late war. The , funeral was attended by the whole of the froope stationed at Or ford Barracks, heeded by the band and firing party, under the command of Captain M. H. B. Morgan, and amongst .many old friends who were pre- sent were Messrs. W. Lennon, ex-Colour-Sergeant, The King's Regiment; W. O'Keeffe, ex-Colour-Sergeant, and J. Roberts, ex-Quartermaster-Sergeant South Lancashire Regiment; and W. Cummins, ex-Sergeant 95th Regiment; also Sergeant-Major G. IT. Ingram, Quartermaster-Sergeant J. Wilcock, and Colour- Sergeant-Instructors J. Allardice and M. Newell, of the 4th (Territorial) Battalion, South Lancashire Regiment. • PENSIONS FOR CORPORATION WORKMEN. The Parliamentary Committee of the St. Helens Corporation have decided to -grant three of their aged work:l:en pensions of 6s. per week, pending the comple- tion of superannuation for the Corporation workmen. It has also been decided to prepare a report on the whole of the workmen, with a view to making some old-age provision for all such workmen who attain tiie age of sixty-flve years.

ALDERMAN BENNETT and the SWAN SONG OF THE DAWN. --- With sincere regret we hare read the last number of "The Dawn." - It is to be deplored that a local paper inspired by such ideals Should go under. The character of the Editor as revealed by "The Dawn" , is an interesting study. The dominating traits are seldom found in combination. Alderman Bennett is sometimes thought .of as One who never knows his ' own mind. He is the despair of party politicians who fumble after programmes as ~a substitute for prin- ciples; to the Conservatives, who claim his allegiance, he is a perpetual conundrum,. they cannot understand how one who can plead so eloquently for Tariff Reform from the .Imperial standpoint, should turn round and support the Licensing Bill and I hammer the House of Lords for its rejection. Nor would the Alderman be less a riddle I to the Liberals were he to return to their fold. In such a party he would constantly be reproaching them for what he would deem to be their base insularity, and he would be at variance with the individualists who among the older school of Liberals are still a force. In his Social sympathies ho would be most at home with the Socialists, with whose aims he has much in common, but his weakness as a practical Socialist would reveal itself when forced to defend the measures by which Socialists try to attain their ends, in the same way as his weakness reveals itself in his advocacy of Tariff Reform as a road to Imperialism. The Alderman's mind in its build and range is not specially adapted to deal with the economic phases which come up whenever these high aims can take shape in plans of economic change. His Imperialism can work with the Imperialism of 1 the Conservatives as long as they both dwell in the pure atmosphere of great ideals, but as soon as the latter takes definite form and shows its feet of clay there is a revolt. The Imperialism of the Editor of "The Dawn "is that of William Watson more than of Kipling. Kipling's " far flung battle line " has little attraction to Mr. Bennett. lie scorns the " common loveless lust of territory, the lips that only babble of their mart." •

STOCKTON HEATit POOR CHILDREN'S TEA AND ENTERTAINMENT.—A pleasing and interesting function took place on Satur- day in the Church room, Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, when 500 of the poorer children of the Parish were entertained to a substantial tea and entertainment. By the kind permission of Mr. W. E. Ray, the Garden Society's Orchestra gave several selections from four to six, which made the little ones happy and cheerful during tea. The Ladies Committee consisting of Mrs. F. A. Jenkins and Miss A. Baxter, assisted by Mesdames Mountield, Sherburn and Brayshaw, worked hard to give the children a treat which has proved a great success and will be renslrabered for years to come. Tea was served at 5 p.m. and helpers were numerous and willing. Among the many we noticed were Mrs. Vere Davies, Miss Joyce, the Vicar, Rev. J. Collins, Nev. C. Harvey and Mrs. Cook, Mrs. T.Baxter' Miss Baxter,Mr.and Mrs. F. Lowe, Miss Crane,Miss A. E. Jenkins, Mr.and Mrs.J. McDermid, Mrs. Rowbottom, Mr. and Mrs. A. Worrall Mr. R. and Miss Jones, Mrs. Tanner, Mrs. Rowson' Mr G. Grounds, Mr. Brayshaw, Miss lienworthy, Mrs Darbyshire, Miss Mounfield, ?krt.. C. P. Roscoe, Miss I?' Noble, Nurse Roscoe and Mr. J. and Miss Hallows After tea each child was given a packet of sweets, and oranges were also distributed. The entertainment pro- gramme bad been provided by Mr. F. A. Jenkins and was of a humorous character. Rev. J. Collins officiated as chairman during the first part and the Rev. C. H. Cook the latter. The following gentlemen kindly entertained, Mr. B. Spruce with his noted Susie's Sous' Band and the rendering of his songs " Oh the agony rt and " Can't you go farther than that " caused great amusement. Mr. R. Scarisbrick with his dolls and musical instruments, and Mr. P. Bleasdale in his stump speech on " Babies," Master .1. Sanders with his char- acter coon song, Master J. Nurse, with his songs "And his day's work was done " and " Ha, ha, ha," kept the 1 Ichildren in happyjmood. The star of the evening was Master Richard Lawton, who sang' Donnybrook Fair" and "The sanest o'th family ' and received iwarm encores. Mr. J. F. Jackson was in his usual merry Imood when he sung "When I was a boy at school." Mr. G. Whitfisl.l entertsined with a Lancashire recital which all appreciated. Mr. 11. Smith was the accom- panist. The proceedings were of a highly successful character and great credit is due to all who contributed in any May towards the children's treat and especially the hon. secretary Mr. F. A. Jenkins.
